articles.title: Porting my 1993 Amiga game to Godot, with an LLM reading the 68000 assembly
articles.summary:
These are my notes from porting my Amiga game, which I originally built in Baghdad in 1993 in MC68000 assembly, to Godot, using Claude Fable 5 during last July holiday.  It took an evening! Getting the feel right and shipping it took a few more weekends and evenings.
I spent the last few weeks analyzing what Claude did, feeding it my 33 years of memory of how I built the game, my notes and the git
articles.body:
In 1993, in Baghdad, I built a game called Babylonian Twins on an Amiga 500:
512KB of RAM, no hard drive, plugged into a TV. I was an engineering student in
my twenties. Pure 68000 assembly, every sprite and every scanline by hand.
Murtadha Salman drew the art and Mahir AlSalman composed the music. We were
under sanctions. No internet, no game development resources, just one copy of
the Amiga Hardware Reference Manual, which I used to program the hardware
directly, and electricity a few hours a day. The constant floppy disk swapping
(because of the small memory) and the 50°C summers killed my disk drive three
Left: 1993, on the Amiga. Right: 2026, the same gateway.
On the Amiga, “by hand” means the game doesn’t ask the operating system for
anything while it runs. At startup it saves the interrupt vectors, switches the
OS interrupts off and takes the whole machine:
move.l 	#$dff000,a0			;Base for hardware registers
lea 	save(pc),a1			;Get the system
move.w 	#$4000,intena(A0)		;from the AMIGA
“Get the system from the AMIGA” is my comment, from 1993. From that point on
the display is the game’s own copper list (the Amiga’s programmable video
coprocessor), rewritten on the fly for sprites and sky colours. Tiles move by
writing the blitter’s registers directly and waiting on its done flag. The
joystick is read straight from the hardware port, and the fire button is one
pin on a CIA chip. The OS comes back only between levels, to load the next
level’s files from the disk, and then it’s switched off again.
It was the first commercial game made in Iraq, and for a long time a game very
few people got to play. Commodore collapsed and sanctions scared off
publishers, so the finished game sat on a shelf. An Amiga forum found it in 2008 from my
brother’s YouTube uploads and hunted me down for the disks;
the thread is still there.
That game is finally out. The original 1993 disks are free on itch.io, and the rebuilt version this post is about, the Definitive Edition, is on iOS and Android now and comes to Steam this fall.
The game has been ported once before, by hand, in 2010. The same team
rebuilt it for the iPhone on an engine written from scratch, about 34,000
lines of C++, over months of nights and weekends. Apple and Google featured
it, and it reached over two million downloads. That story is
I didn’t do this port. I asked for it, played the result every night, said
what felt wrong, and made the few decisions that needed somebody who was
there in 1993. The file formats and the assembly reading were the AI’s work,
and so were the decisions about how to carry thirty-year-old code across, and
it went faster than I could follow. This post is what I found when I sat down
weeks later and read what had been done to my own game. Some of it was wrong,
and I didn’t notice for weeks.
I’d tried this before. About a year ago I gave an earlier model the same Amiga
material and asked it to make sense of my binary level maps. It got there in
the end, but it took several rounds and a lot of hints from me.
Then Claude Fable 5 shipped, and I gave it the same files.
The test was deliberate. My guess was that there is little Amiga assembly
code in LLM training sets. If the model was better at working things out
rather than recalling them, this is where it would show.
The July 4th weekend was coming up, so I planned three steps, each one
conditional on the previous working.
Step one, the safe ask: my own 2010 engine, the 34,000 lines of C++, moved
into Godot 4. This was the control.
Step two, the unfair ask: the original 72,758 lines of 68000 assembly, for a
machine that had gone out of production, with no comments to speak of and
nothing in common with the C++. Rebuild that in Godot too, at the Amiga’s
Step three, the greedy ask: put the second one inside the first, so buying the
modern game gets you the 1993 original as a second thing you can launch.
All three worked. The level format that had taken several rounds and my
corrections a year earlier came out in a single pass, with no hints from me.
I ran it in Claude Code, so it had a terminal and my filesystem. It could edit files, run the assembler,
build the game, launch the game and read what came back. When I say below that
it rebuilt my 1993 binaries and checked them, it did that by running vasm and
Early on it added a set of command-line flags to the game so it could play
--level=<name>       load a level directly
--pose=<spec>        put the twins at exact positions
--drive=<spec>       press buttons on a script, frame by frame
--probe              dump switch / gate / door / key state
--screenshot=<path>  render a frame and quit
Which turns “does the jump feel right” into something a machine can read:
drive[btw_jump:2.2] pos=(25.44, 24.04) vel=(0.00, -14.51) ground=false apex_y=22.48
It also had two headless checks it could run before showing me anything: one
that compiles every script, and one that builds every level and reports
failures. On the Amiga side it drove the real toolchain, vasm to assemble and
FS-UAE to boot the result. What wasn’t automated: there was no image
comparison on the modern port (it took screenshots, I looked at them), and
nothing checked whether the game felt right.
Step one: 34,000 lines of C++ in an evening
Wednesday night, the safe ask. Timestamps, unedited:
22:23  Godot 4 project scaffold, asset sync, TMX level pipeline
22:44  both twins playable — collision, physics, camera, switching
23:19  all 38 entity types ported — full object roster live
00:35  full screen flow — menus, map, story, save, game flows
02:15  exporting to macOS, iOS and Android
Twenty-one minutes from empty project to a playable character. Every line it
moved that night was a line I’d written, over months, in 2010. I went to bed
Getting it to feel right took about three days after that: jump arcs and
trampoline timing, and hit detection that rewards mashing, fixed in batches on
July 2nd, 3rd and 4th.
I wasn’t testing alone. My thirteen-year-old son played every build with me.
He’s always known I made this game, it’s a fact about his father he grew up
with, but he’d never seen me working on it. The testing turned into a
father-and-son thing I didn’t plan, and it’s one of my favourite parts of the
All the gameplay state lives in tile units (1.0 = one 48px tile), and the
update runs at a fixed 60 Hz, because the 2010 iOS build ran at 60 Hz. That
matters because the original applies drag multiplicatively, every frame:
static const float GROUND_DRAG_FACTOR = 0.85f;
this->velocity.x *= GROUND_DRAG_FACTOR;   // every tick!
Multiply by 0.85 sixty times a second and you get one amount of friction;
multiply fifty times a second and you get another. Port it to a different tick
rate and every acceleration curve in the game changes. Nothing crashes, it
just feels wrong forever, and you won’t find it by reading the diff. At 60 Hz
the constant transplants verbatim. This is also why the 1993 rebuild runs at
50 Hz and the modern one at 60: two sets of hand-tuned numbers, each only
correct at its own tick. It kept both clocks. I’d have been tempted to tidy
Godot ships CharacterBody2D and move_and_slide(), and every tutorial tells
you to use them. The port used neither for the player. The original has its
own hand-written movement code, and rebuilding that on somebody else’s physics
would feel slightly wrong in ways that are miserable to track down. The player
is a plain Node2D, and the 150-line collision routine came across line for
line, including the fudge numbers I picked by feel fifteen years ago and the
comments I wrote to my future self:
# Add 0.5 because we want the character's feet to be in the middle of the tile.
var bottom := pos.y + dim.y / 2 + 0.5 + i + fraction
if int(bottom) == int(pos.y + dim.y / 2 + 0.49):
var left := pos.x - dim.x / 4      # asymmetric probes!
Nothing tidied up the stray 0.49. There are no tests and no docs; those
Step two: the 68000 assembly
By Sunday afternoon, July 5th, I handed over the thing I actually wanted to
test. 72,758 lines across 26 files, written for a machine with 512 KB of
memory, by me, for me, with the commenting habits of somebody who never
expected another person to read it. No documentation. A 2008 transfer to
modern storage had shortened every long filename, so every include pointed at
names that no longer existed. One of the five level source files is cut off
partway through a data table. There’s no other copy.
Before porting anything, it made the 1993 sources assemble again, using vasm
on an Apple Silicon Mac, and kept going until the output was byte-identical
to the binaries that shipped.
14:34  import the Amiga sources, assets, references
14:49  vasm toolchain reproduces the shipped binaries byte-identically
15:42  the rebuilt demo boots and plays in FS-UAE
Fifteen minutes from a folder of files to the first rebuild that matched the
shipped bytes. I wrote these in ASM-One, whose dialect differs from vasm’s in ways that change the bytes:
ASM-One encodes cmp #4,d0 as CMPI, vasm picks a different, equally valid
encoding, so telling it not to optimise is necessary and not sufficient.
Rather than edit my sources it wrote a preprocessing pass that bridges five
such differences, and rebuilt the broken filename mapping file by file.
The expensive one was org. With no linker and no relocation, the level
source lays out the Amiga’s memory by hand, address by address:
org $6a000				; this section lives at address $6a000
org mapadd+73*1024		; skip to 73 KB past the map's start
dc.w $3333,50,20,100		; one object record begins
org glbtable+2*1024			; the object table gets exactly 2 KB
The level-one map uses 74,400 of those 74,752 bytes, a margin of 352, and
nothing checked it except me, in 1993. (SahamR-grb attaches an object’s
behaviour as a named offset; saham is Arabic for arrow.) ASM-One’s
org can also move the location counter backwards, which vasm can’t. The
first workaround got one case wrong: a ds.b 800 inside a rewound block,
which ASM-One treats as “skip 800 bytes”, was written out as 800 bytes of
zeros. Everything after that point in the file, the copper list included, sat
944 bytes away from where the shipped binary had it. The game assembled and
booted, and drew the wrong thing.
Even after that, some chunks still wouldn’t match, by about 108 bytes
scattered through the variable area. Those bytes explained where the shipped
files came from. ASM-One assembles into memory, and the game got onto disk by
saving that memory out, after the game had been run. So the shipped files are
a snapshot of a game that had already been running, not clean assembler
output. A fresh assembly has zeros in those variables, because nothing has set
them yet; the shipped disk has whatever they held on the machine when it was
saved. The code writes them before it reads them, so the zeros are harmless.
At the time I read that line, moved on, and waited for the actual game. It
took me weeks to see that this was the most important thing in the project,
and that nobody had asked for it. From then on, every claim about this game
could be settled by comparing bytes. I wouldn’t have done it myself. I
already had the binaries, and in eighteen years rebuilding them from source
never seemed worth an afternoon.
For every format it went to the code that reads the bytes and worked
backwards from that. The level loader is 1,652 lines of uncommented 68000,
which is why I’d always reached for a hex editor instead.
A level is a grid of tiles: a long list of numbers, where each number means
“put picture 47 here”, in my own private 1993 layout. This is the format the
older model and I had ground through a year earlier.
Here is the full set of tiles a level is built from, 256 of them, 16×16
pixels each, for level one:
And a slice of level one, assembled from those tiles:
The input is a list of numbers with no header and no dimensions, inside a
compressed chunk. This time I didn’t explain anything.
It found the drawing routine, read how the grid was walked, worked out the
width and height from constants elsewhere in the file, and produced correct
maps for all five levels on the first attempt.
Then it re-rendered each level from its own extracted data and compared the
result, pixel by pixel, against full-level captures I had made in 2020. Where
they didn’t match, it went looking for the cause and found two copper
effects: the sky gradient and the water colour cycle. With those two accounted
for: five full-level images, zero differing
pixels. Level one alone is 600 tiles wide, 9,600 pixels.
Drawing the level is only half of what a map cell does. Each cell is one
16-bit word, and the picture is the smaller part of it:
one map cell, 16 bits:
bits 15..10   the property: what this square DOES       (6 bits)
bit 8         which of the two tile banks to use        (1 bit)
bits 7..0     which of the 256 tile pictures to draw    (8 bits)
The property is the level’s invisible physics. 1 is solid ground. 2 and 3 can
be climbed. 10 to 13 all mean “this hurts”, four codes because knockback needs
a direction. 14 kills outright. 63 is a door. None of this is written down
anywhere. It was recovered because two routines read the same word and each
one reveals its own half: the draw loop masks off the low byte, and the
collision check does the opposite:
move.w	(a1),d6			; the same cell
and.w	#$fc00,d6		; keep the top 6 bits
lsr.w	#8,d6			; d6 = the property, 0..63
bsr	cbCheck			; 2 or 3?  you can climb this
bsr	Checkrmh		; 10..13?  this hurts, and from which side
Checkrmh hands the painful cases to a label called rmhEnjury, which is
Those bits were painted in an editor. Before the game could be built I had to
build the tool that builds it: MEDITOR.S, 1,254 lines of assembly, dated by
its own header, in my 1993 English:
; *		This Program was written in four days			*
; *      I made it to help me to make a map to my first serious		*
Four days in February 1993. Paint tiles with the mouse, pick a property number
on the panel’s CURRENT FLAG counter, stamp it onto cells with PUT FLAG, and a
flag view marks every cell carrying the selected number. While writing this
post, I asked the model to run the map editor and get a screenshot. It
assembled the 1993 source with a modern assembler, laid the shipped Level 2
data out in memory where the editor expects it, and booted the result in an
My own tool at thirty-three years old, editing the real Level 2, flag view on.
CURRENT FLAG reads 0001, solid, and the ground you can stand on is marked
while the decoration you walk through isn’t. The panel says 1994: the panel
artwork is a separate bitmap file the editor loads, and the copy that survived
is a later one than the February 1993 code.
The other name on the panel, Udai, was my partner in Mesopotamia Software,
which is what we called ourselves. He was building a game of his own at the
time. I wrote the editor, for both of us, but its design was worked out
between us so one tool could serve both games. His game was never finished.
Enemies aren’t in the map. The world is stored one screen at a time, 25 tiles by 20, and every screen has a
small table of the objects on it. My 1993 comments explain the markers:
;	$1111=this is a Screen but it contain nothing or(End of Screen)
;	$2222=this is an object but do not draw it (dead)go to next
;	other=this is an object,draw it and go to the next
Scr0:	dc.w $3333,50,23,17		; a live object: frame, then x, y
dc.w hiddenwallR-lrb,20		; its behaviour: a routine, as an offset
dc.w 10				; parameters only that routine understands
dc.w $1111			; end of this screen
An enemy is a row of words: a marker, a frame, a position inside its screen,
then its behaviour. hiddenwallR-lrb is the crumbling-wall routine, attached
as an offset from a base label, the same trick as the arrow thrower earlier.
The words after it are parameters that mean whatever that routine wants them
to mean. Nothing in the file says which word is which, so it found the routine
that walks these tables every frame and let it name the fields, then converted
every object in all five levels to world coordinates and checked them against
Most of the data files scramble their 16-byte headers with a key stored inside
the file, a 1993 trick to keep disk editors out. The retail loader, GAME.S,
has no unscrambling step at all. It read that as a clue: GAME.S was
written before the scrambling was added,
so it is an older file. That clue is what later let it recover the lost
two-disk retail set, from a sector map inside that same file.
The doors aren’t in the map
I was sure they were.
Load a level’s tile map and there are holes where every door should be, with
no door tile in them, open or closed. An 18-byte object record stamps them onto
the map at runtime, a 1×4 tile column, from a table:
closed  $528  $53C  $550  $564      ; solid, blocks the way
open    $129  $13D  $151  $165      ; passable — exactly one sheet-column right
The map data says there’s no door. The level code says there is. For
thirty-three years I’d have told you the map is the source of truth and doors
are map data, and I’d never have looked. It held both facts, found the routine
that reconciles them, and came back with the design: doors are drawn by code
at runtime; they were never painted into the map in the editor. That’s why
the obvious port of the level data produces a tower with doorways full of
In every level, colour index 31 is the sky, and nothing in the tile art ever
paints it. The tile atlas renders it transparent, and behind it the copper
repaints the background colour on chosen scanlines to make a vertical
gradient. The gradient sits in the level source as a plain list of colours.
This is the entire sky of the second level:
Read down the list and the sky goes from pale blue to warm near the horizon.
The same 24 words, rendered. Left is the top of the screen.
The first rebuild missed it, and the levels looked fine. Flat, in a way I
couldn’t name. The pixel comparison refused to go green, and the gradient went
The diff that would not go green: white is every pixel the first rebuild got wrong, the copper's sky and water.
Amiga sprite sheets are planar (five separate 1-bit bitplanes in plane-major
strips, plus a transparency mask), and all of that was worked out from the
draw routines and the org arithmetic. Sheet sizes of the form frames * width * height * 2 * 5 are
ambiguous: that 2 could mean double-width frames, or two stacked rows, one
per facing direction. Both readings fit every byte in the file. It’s two
facing rows; that was my choice in 1993.
Two stacked rows, one per facing direction, drawn frame by frame, not mirrored.
It flagged the ambiguity and asked.
The same twin, the same six frames: 1993 above, 2026 below.
That was the last format. From there the 1993 game went into Godot the same
way the C++ had, behaviour rewritten in GDScript at the original 50 Hz.
Step three: the old game inside the new one
The greedy ask took one evening, 21:58 to 23:43. The retro game runs as a
guest, with its own namespace and scene host, and the engine switches to
50 Hz on the way in and back to 60 on the way out. It’s fiddly, and it was
done in one sitting. I’d assumed the feature would eat a week and get cut.
It’s the reason the Steam version ships with the 1993 game inside
The same doorway in both games, running in the same program. Left: 1993. Right: 2026.
The game you download contains no Amiga code. The data, the packed chunks and planar graphics
and the music, was decoded once, on my machine, by Python scripts, into
ordinary PNG, WAV and JSON. The behaviour (how a guard patrols, when a door
opens) was rewritten in the engine’s own language. If you want the real
thing, that’s the free disk image at the end of this post and
In level 2 you walk along a corridor. Waterfall to your left, stone pillar
ahead. No enemy on the screen, nothing approaching, and you take a hit. What
hit you was a spear-carrying soldier standing thirteen tiles above you, on a
grass ledge next to a palm tree, with solid rock in between.
He’s a doorman. He shoves whoever stands at his feet. In the original that
check is fenced on both sides:
sub.w   d1,d4           ; d4 = vertical distance to the kid
bpl     Sg.Far          ; 4 or more rows below? not my problem
bmi     SG.far          ; too far above? also not my problem
The port kept the lower bound and dropped the upper one. A shove meant to
cover the guard’s own three rows now ran the whole height of the map column
beneath him, through the floor, into a corridor he doesn’t appear in.
The doorman himself, from the 1993 sheet.
Smaller ones: every level has a second tile layer the original never
renders; it’s the hidden artwork revealed when a door opens or a fake wall
crumbles. Render it “faithfully” and every secret passage stands open from
the start. Move enemies before players instead of after, and a trampoline jump
gets counted twice, twenty tiles into the air. A door listed "p1,p2,p3,p4",
meaning all four palms, was read as a single key with a strange name, and the
tutorial exit never opened. A sound-loop length computed as stereo when the
effects are mono cut every sound off halfway and restarted it.
The one that cost the most was a feature I asked for in the 1993 build: let
the twins swap places at any distance. The proximity check came out, and the
statues started corrupting. It went back into the routine and came out with the real
answer, which wasn’t what I expected: that check was never a distance
limit. The idle twin is stamped into the map itself as a statue, and
two statues stamped on top of each other eat each other’s tiles. The guard
went back in, and I killed the feature on the 1993 build.
I made the same kind of mistake myself in 2010, slowly, over months.
Then it did the release work: screenshots at five pixel sizes in eleven
languages, a preview video, store text, icons in six shapes, uploaded to three
stores that disagree about everything. I’ve shipped this game before, so I
know how many evenings that part costs.
The screenshots come out of the game itself. It launches the real game at each
store’s pixel size, in the language it needs, walks the character to a chosen
spot, takes the shot, then draws the caption band with the game’s own fonts.
AI never renders the text in a store image. The captions are real fonts and
real translated strings, or the image doesn’t ship. Once it did break, and the
Russian and Korean captions came out as rows of empty boxes, which I saw in
the output folder before uploading.
My complaint about Steam is that it has many fields in its forms, many more
than the Apple App Store and the Google Play Console. In addition, it doesn’t
have an API to make the process of metadata updates easy. For iOS and Android
there are proper APIs and it used them. Steam has a web dashboard, so it drove
the browser: store page fields, achievements, the demo checklist, artwork
uploads, clicking through Steamworks. I do the login, and I
press anything that submits, publishes, prices or releases. It fills in the
It reads my reviews too. The official Google Play API only gives you the last
seven days, which is useless for a game with fifteen years of reviews, so it
pulls the rest with the public scraper, one language at a time. Then it read all of them and listed which ones
described real defects. I approved the list.
One of them was a one-star review on Google Play, bad spelling, the kind you
“cant get through door on level one. opens but level dowsnt end”
Read literally, it’s a bug report, and it was right. In my game, opening
the exit and walking through it are two separate actions, and the prompt that
says so exists in all eleven languages, placed in exactly two of my eighteen
levels. One of the levels missing it was the last free one. So the player
deciding whether this game is worth paying for was standing in front of an
open door with no way to know what to do, and concluded the game was broken.
I never found that in fifteen years, and neither did my testers or two
rebuilds. It took a stranger’s one-star review. The fix went out as 2.0.3 on both
stores. I keep that review.
“The trampoline feels too high.” That was the whole report, from me, playing
the build at night. The
constants checked out: a twenty-line simulation of the original’s integrator
predicted 19.1 tiles, and the build measured 19.5. The physics was right.
It was input semantics. The 2010 build was event-driven, and because of a
workaround for a tvOS quirk we shipped years ago, a held jump button read as
released until you physically pressed again. Godot polls input, and kept
reporting the hold. Reproducing that accident is what makes the high bounce
need a fresh, well-timed press, which is how the game played on a phone, and
what my hands were expecting.
The 2010 source doesn’t record this, because from the source’s point of view
nothing unusual is happening. You’d have to have been
there, holding the phone, working around a bug in a television.
After thirty-three years, the full original is out, free on
itch.io. Boot it in FS-UAE,
WinUAE, or on real hardware. The Definitive Edition is on iOS and Android now,
has a free demo on Steam, and the full Steam release (Windows, Mac, Linux)
lands this fall, with the 1993 game inside it as a second launch option.
The port was Claude Fable 5 running in Claude Code; I asked, played, and
decided. This post went the same way. I gave it my notes from the port, what
I remember about the key parts of the old game (the map encoding, the object
tables), and the repos for both the Amiga version and the port, and it wrote
a first draft. I spent a week editing it line by line. The code, timestamps
and screenshots are real. The part I’m least sure of is the 108 bytes: the
model told me the shipped files were a memory snapshot saved after a run, and
that the code writes those variables before it reads them. I read that, moved
on, and have never checked it myself.
One slice from each of the five levels, rendered from the extracted map data.
Babylonian Twins: Definitive Edition comes to Steam this fall —
Free demo available now · live today on iOS and Android · the original 1993
ADF is free on itch.

articles.title: They were raised on Drag Race UK - but can they snatch the crown?
articles.summary: A new wave of queens raised on the hit reality show are among the 12 contestants set to compete for the series eight crown.
articles.body: They were raised on Drag Race UK - but can they snatch the crown?Image source, BBC/World of Wonder/Nick StrasburgImage caption, Mocha says Drag Race inspired her to get into drag ByNaomi ClarkeBBC NewsbeatA new batch of queens from across the UK are set to battle it out in the hope of hearing RuPaul's magical words: "Condragulations, you're a winner, baby". The UK edition of Drag Race has been putting hopeful contestants through their paces for seven years - plenty of time for a new wave of talent raised on the hit reality show to emerge. Now "Generation Ru" are ready to compete for the crown and £25,000 cash prize.Series eight contestant Mocha, 26, tells BBC Newsbeat she considers herself part of this new cohort.  "My drag has always been inspired by Drag Race because that's why I started," the Essex-born queen says. "I think watching Drag Race made me realise that all of these things that I grew up wanting to do - like be a fashion designer, be a singer, like be a dancer, do makeup - it's actually all these things combined and I can be all of them at once." Image source, BBC/World of Wonder/Nick StrasburgImage caption, Flesh is fighting for the crown after her best friend Bones took the title last seasonMocha, who describes herself as a "fashion clown" and musical theatre lover, says it has taken her nearly a decade to get to this stage but feels it is the "right time".And while watching the show has influenced her style and given her a something to work towards, she says the process isn't for those who just want to get on TV."Drag is hard and you've got to love it, you've got to have a passion for it," she says. "Drag Race is the extra-special prize you get at the end, but it's not the main goal in that way." London-based queen and fellow contestant Flesh agrees she is "100% Generation Ru"."I found drag through queens who had featured in the American franchise," the 26-year-old says. "And from the first season of the UK franchise I was hooked, I was a fan."It has always really been my blueprint.“She has also developed her "supermodel of Soho" style alongside her best friend Bones, the reigning Drag Race UK Superstar.Flesh says she was "so happy" for her drag sister when she won, but it also made her "terrified" to compete this year as she focused on proving herself. Image source, BBC/World of Wonder/Nick StrasburgImage caption, Naya Thorn says the expense of preparing for the show almost led her to drop-outAlmost 100 queens have lip-synced their way through Drag Race UK's challenges, but there are fans who worry whether the British scene can support more series of the annual show.Series eight's youngest contestant, Naya Thorn, who was 23 when she was chosen for the show, feels there are new queens cropping up all over the UK.But she admits the show would benefit if more "seasoned and colourful characters" from across the scene got involved.However, she says, cost-of-living pressures are putting a strain on queens trying to make it.Naya, from Dudley, West Midlands, says the expense of preparing for the show almost led her to drop-out, and she wouldn't have been TV-ready without her support network at home."It really upsets me that there's a lot of people that would do well on the show and should have that platform that feel like they can't go on because of how expensive it seems to be getting," she says. "But I am here to prove to everyone, you don't need that much money." Image source, BC/World of Wonder/Nick StrasburgImage caption, Series eight contestant Paris Baby feels the new season will usher in a "drag renaissance"Flesh, who has been running a drag show for the past five years, says she has also seen turnout at live performances drop, and feels soaring costs have likely impacted that. She thinks the TV show still appeals as it provides "the joy and the power of drag from the comfort of your own home", but says this comes at a price to performers."Expectations remain at a Drag Race level and our income and opportunities in the real world do not reflect that," she says. The Soho-based queen also says social media has become a "double-edged sword".Although it's vital to advertise live shows, "the more you show... the less inclined people are to go", she says.Flesh adds: "If the public aren't willing to support drag outside of the Drag Race vehicle" then "we won't be able to sustain Drag Race".The queens this year will be hoping to spark more interest into the show and drag, including Paris Baby, who describes herself as "UK's British Bajan Barbie".She has been hailing the new series as the "drag renaissance" as she feels it was a "really strong" year and hopes it will be "very well received" internationally."Hopefully we can bring a little 'je ne sais quoi' and reignite the interest in drag," she says.RuPaul's Drag Race UK series eight launches at 22:00 BST on BBC Three and is available to watch on BBC iPlayer.Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.More on this story

articles.title: Hohem’s tiny steadycam has a removable action cam

articles.body:
Hohem is trying something new with its Eyepic handheld stabilized camera to differentiate it from existing offerings from companies like DJI and Insta360. At its core, the camera is functionally similar to devices like the Osmo Pocket 4 and Insta360 Luna Ultra with a rotating preview screen and a small camera module stabilized by a three-axis gimbal. But the Eyepic borrows an idea popularized by recent action cams by letting you detach the magnetic camera module and use it as a tiny standalone camera you can mount or wear.
The Eyepic captures 4K video at up to 60fps in a vertical or horizontal orientation that can be changed by rotating the 2.51-inch touchscreen display on its grip, which also includes a joystick for manually adjusting framing and a lever for changing the zoom level. Details on battery life, built-in storage, tracking capabilities, and pricing haven’t been shared yet.
[Image: The Eyepic comes with accessories for clipping the camera module to clothing like hats or wearing it using a magnetic lanyard. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/hohem2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
To capture more dynamic hands-free footage, the Eyepic camera can be used on its own clipped to clothing, worn using an included lanyard, or magnetically attached to compatible surfaces. The tiny action cam lacks a screen of its own but streams a live 1080p preview to the Eyepic’s touchscreen that can be used to preview framing or remotely adjust settings up to 32 feet away. The grip and gimbal aren’t water-friendly, but the action cam module is completely waterproof to a depth of just over 32 feet.

articles.body:
Today, I’m talking with Tom Conrad, the CEO of Sonos. Tom and I have known each other for a long time — he was the chief technology officer of Pandora, VP of product at Snap, and the chief product officer of Quibi. He was also on the board at Sonos during its disastrous 2024 app redesign that threatened to crash the entire brand. 
Tom took over as interim CEO to right the ship during that period, and then took the permanent role just about a year ago. As you’ll hear him say, he thinks Sonos is fully out of that period now, and on to its next chapter with a huge product and platform launch called Sonos 27.
I mean, come on, you all listen to the show. That is all the most Decoder bait imaginable. I have been dying to have Tom on the show to talk about how the board decided to move on from previous CEO Patrick Spence, how he diagnosed the issues inside the company, and what decisions he made to fix them.
Those fixes involved a lot of big changes: to the company’s structure, its product lineup, and how it thinks about itself and what its product fundamentally is. That’s that new platform, Sonos 27, which you’ll hear Tom call a new foundation for the company that makes every Sonos product work better as part of a system. 
There’s a lot here, including how AI assistants can work across the system, the idea of having a mesh network of little computers in your home disguised as speakers, and of course, the testy relationship between Sonos and Google, which means Google’s Gemini assistant isn’t available on Sonos devices. 
Oh, and of course we got into the weeds about smart home standards, because I am a smart home nerd and simply cannot help myself. But to his credit, Tom was willing to nerd out with me, and I think this conversation is pretty fun because of it.
Okay: Sonos CEO Tom Conrad. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. 
Tom Conrad, you’re the CEO of Sonos. Welcome to Decoder.
Thank you. As they say, it’s so great to be here.
I am just going to say, finally, I have been asking you to be on the show for at least a year, if not before. I think the first time I met you was in the back of a car at CES when you were at Pandora.
One hundred years ago. We were children.
[Laughs] We were little babies. That car was driven by a human driver. That’s how far back it was.
And then you took a turn through Quibi. You and I talked through that, and now you’re at Sonos. As you know, I’m a huge fan of Sonos. We had your predecessor, Patrick Spence, on the show a bunch of times. 
Many things have happened, so I just want to start at the very beginning of this. You’re about a year into being the permanent CEO of Sonos. You have a bunch of news to announce. Just tell us what you think Sonos is today. What is your conception of this company?
When I came in the door, one of my earliest observations was that the company behaved like it was 100 percent hardware, but we’re really 100 percent hardware and 100 percent software. And if you get either one of those even a little bit wrong, the impact is tremendous.
So how does that show up really day-to-day? It was about returning the company to the idea that Sonos doesn’t make these individual products, but we really make one thing — we make the Sonos system. It all has to hang together in a cohesive, interesting, and valuable way, or we’re just not doing the work. 
There’s been a bunch of basic blocking and tackling, of course, both operationally and in the work that we’re doing in the product family. But at the highest level, returning the company to the idea that we are a system for audio in the home has been the highest-level mantra.
When you say come into the company, do you mean as a board member or as the CEO?
I mean, let’s start the starter pistol in January of 2025, 18 months ago, when I stepped in first as interim CEO and then was lucky enough six months later to be asked to take the job more permanently.
The reason I asked that question is that you obviously have two different views of the company in different roles. We did have former CEO Patrick Spence on several occasions, and he said something very similar to me when he first took over — that Sonos was stuck in its ways. It was really focused on very, very slow iterations of hardware. 
He tried very hard to push the metabolism of the company to be much faster, and he talked about that very openly with me. That led eventually to what I think is a moment of true crisis: the app launch. It was a disaster. The system stopped working. That’s when you came in to right the ship.
Tell me about that gap. You came in, and you said this company thinks it’s a hardware company. That’s what your predecessor had been saying, but it went sideways in big, meaningful ways. Tell me about that moment and why you think it was the same conception even when you came in.
So as you describe, I’ve been involved with the company going back almost 20 years. We brought Pandora to Sonos in 2007, I think, and I was able to get to know the company as a partner before I got to know it as a board member. I came onto the board in 2016 right as Patrick became CEO. So from the vantage point of a board member, I got to participate in Patrick’s chapter.
I guess the way I would characterize his high-order thinking about the company in those early days was that, as you described, he wanted to turn the company into a product execution machine with an emphasis on hardware products. We call them NPIs, or new product introductions.
In the chapter before him, it was sometimes years between new Sonos products. Spence said, “Look, we’re going to make a company that knows how to ship a couple of great new products a year.” And he did that. I mean, the company has reliably shipped a couple of great products, hardware products, every year, for close to a decade now.
Sometimes, when you energize an organization around an idea, there are unintended consequences. I think one unintended consequence of that framing was that the company became very focused on the individual products, one at a time. Even as a board member, I received Roam as a portable speaker with a certain amount of battery life, waterproofing, and Bluetooth connectivity. I didn’t really think about it as a member of the Sonos system. 
Even with the software work that we did, and with every product that we make, there is a tremendous amount of software effort and innovation that goes into them. But even the software that we made was very focused on the individual NPIs. “What can we do in software to differentiate Move 2 from other speakers in that category?”
What was hard to do, and what was hard to prioritize in the company, was horizontal slices of software experiences that benefited all of the platform. So, in a way, I think some of that debt accumulated, and the company thought that the antidote was to recreate the app experience. And as you know, we made a bunch of mistakes at that moment.
I’m really proud of the fact that I think we’re well beyond that chapter now, but we could have been much more thoughtful about how we qualified that product in the real world. We could have been much more thoughtful about how we rolled it out to customers. We could have, candidly, I think, examined the original impetus in the first place. It was very Sonos-motivated. We wanted to put the app on a modern architecture to make us more nimble.
In my chapter at Sonos, I’m really trying to bring it all back to how we can focus on the customer first. I’m so inspired by talking to people on social media and in my inbox, and people in the industry, like you, about how we show up and solve the real problems that are happening in real households. I’m so excited about the things we’re going to talk to you about today because I think they’re really an answer to many of those questions.
If you’re a listener, you know I’m familiar with Tom. The man’s on Threads doing customer support every day. And actually, I should not take advantage of this. I hold myself back from asking you for direct customer support all the time.
Anytime. The way that you can tell it’s actually me and not our crackerjack social team is that I often will let a Thread die before I should or fail to follow up with someone. So if we were executing perfectly on that, you would know it was fake Tom, but it’s real Tom, and I do it when I can, but sometimes imperfectly.
At least it’s not an AI avatar Tom. That’s when we know it’s going to go sideways.
I know you’re a Decoder fan, so I’m going to make you sit in this for just one more moment because I find all of this to be really fascinating. The app shipped, and the feedback was immediately and intensely negative. Many, many things were broken. Speakers weren’t working at weddings. This is a time of massive crisis. 
The company goes to resolve it, but then you’re on the board, and it’s clear that there’s going to be a leadership transition, that Patrick needs to go, and we need a new CEO. You’re going to be the interim CEO. 
Tell us about that process. Very, very few people will ever be in that kind of process or get insight into that process. What happened? What were the steps?
Well, I guess you start by saying that the last thing as a board that you want to do is to remove a CEO, particularly one who had as many successes as Patrick had. But I think as we looked at the company’s progress recovering from the app crisis, and frankly the tenor of the conversation inside the company, we just decided that for this kind of step-function improvement we needed on some of these dimensions, we had to make some changes in leadership, and that included a CEO change.
It was a wild experience for me because, I’ll tell you, at no point in the decade leading up to that day in January did I imagine that I might end up the CEO of Sonos. But in the process, the board asked if I’d be willing to step in on an interim basis, and it was an easy yes for me. It’s a cliché, but I’m a customer, and I love this product. There was a Sonos Move in the room when my daughter was born. You talked about weddings. I was watching friends and colleagues on the internet, frustrated by their experience. I wanted to come in and fix it. Of course, as a board member, I felt some real culpability in it. So [I was] thrilled at the chance to come in.
When you’re an interim CEO, the assignment is really to keep the wheels on. The assignment at Sonos specifically was to right the ship. So during the period when the board was doing their comprehensive search for the person that they would ultimately decide was the right choice for the company, it was really easy for me to show up and just do that hard work of trying to get the company back on track. 
While I never imagined that I would land in this seat, I feel so blessed that it happened. I do love this job and continue to love the company and the team, and I’m so excited about the things we’re doing for our customers.
Very few people are going to get an interview to become the CEO of Sonos. I imagine at some point you went from being the interim CEO to wanting to become the permanent CEO. What was that process like? Did you write a memo? Was there a pitch deck? What were the steps?
Yeah, so there were a couple of pitch moments that the board asked me, completely reasonably, to engage in the process of applying for the job in the same way that all of the other talented candidates that they spoke to engaged. And so I took a personality test. 
Like an ENTJ or whatever?
Oh, yeah. One of the letter things, sure. They wanted to know what they were getting.
Do they know that that is basically just like astrology? Someone should tell them.
You know what? Yep, yep. I presented my vision for the company more than once, and I had the incredible advantage of being inside the four walls of the company and deeply understanding what was working and what wasn’t, and the things that we needed to do to get to this next chapter. It was a period of intense, intense work for me and everybody around me at the company, and more than a little anxiety about how it was going to turn out.
It was so fun, though, to get the call and then to just immediately be able to pivot at least a fraction of the work from the entirely tactical to the much more strategic, to begin to talk about what kind of company we are going to build together in this next chapter.
When it was announced that you would become the permanent CEO, even when you were the interim CEO, my reaction was, “Oh, this makes sense.” To use a football analogy, football teams hire defensive head coaches and offensive head coaches, and they come from one side of the ball or the other. It was just obvious: “Oh, this company needs a software CEO, and Tom is a software guy.” 
You’re describing a situation where obviously it’s both. You’ve got hardware and software together, but that was the light that went off in my head — “Oh, this is a software person coming in to fix a big software problem.” Is that how you saw it initially?
Yeah, my career started with selling personal computers in 1986 or something, at the original Micro Center. If you’ve ever been to a Micro Center, it’s one of the few remaining big-box retailers for computers. So at the original Micro Center in Columbus, Ohio, at 16 years old, I walked into the CEO’s office and said, “I want to work here.” So from my earliest days, I was sitting with early adopters of personal computers and watching their struggles to understand the technology and put it to use in their lives.
I became an engineer and a product designer out of a desire to help people learn to use these products. And that’s really what’s motivated me through my entire career: how do I help teams make great experiences? So while it’s true that I’m a software person, 35 years in the business, my identity really is as a product designer. And I’d like to think that the board imagined that, yes, they needed a software person, but they needed somebody who could holistically look at the opportunity across hardware and software and help the team get there.
You appear to be through it now. There’s a big stack of announcements here, including MCP integration. I’ve got a lot of questions about all that. 
When you became the permanent CEO 18 months ago, you said you immediately shifted strategy. What brought that into focus for you? “Oh, this is actually a software platform with hardware components”? Was that instinct? Was it research? Was it, “I’m getting through this app process, and that is becoming revealed to me”? How did that work?
I think by disposition I’m a fairly right-brained person, and I have this intuitive feeling — creative, or whatever the words are, not as quantitative. But my first job out of college was at Apple, and I think even from the early days when I was there, we talked about the intersection of the arts and humanities and the sciences. 
I think one lesson of my career has been that you really do have an obligation to bring both a quant and a qual assessment to most things that pass your desk. So the development of our strategy was very much like that. Yes, there was an intuitive sense about what the right answer for Sonos was that was built up from my experience as a customer by observing our customers and talking to them through the years. A piece of that is a perspective about where the puck is going, of course.
But I do have access to piles and piles and piles of data about how our products behave in the real world, how our customers interact with them, what they use, what they don’t use, and lots of people around me in the organization who can bring that quantitative framing. I think one advantage I had over other CEO candidates was that I could bring some of that horsepower to bear on the story that I shared with the board about my vision for the future of the company.
You’ve made some changes. It’s time for the Decoder questions. You have restructured the company. There have been a few rounds of layoffs. How big is Sonos today?
And how is that structured?
So the company that I stepped into was divided into business units. We had a team that was focused on home. We had a team that was focused on the professional opportunity, a team that was focused on home theater, and so on. While there’s something to be said for P&L responsibilities, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera, there’s something to be said for that approach at a certain scale. I think that my appraisal was that we were sub-scale for the inefficiencies that creep in. We have the almost guaranteed duplication of effort across the silos.
What’s more, if you imagine that the product is really the system, the idea that your portables team sits far away from your home theater team, and sits far away from your plugged-in speakers team, is almost surely going to run counter to the kind of progress that you’re trying to motivate. And so very quickly, within three weeks of my arrival, we reorganized the company into a functional model.
So my leadership team today, of course, has a finance organization, a legal organization, a sales organization, and a marketing organization. But the product team now shows up as represented by hardware, software, and global supply chain operations, so leaders across each of those things. And what that allows us to do is to assemble cross-functional teams, or matrix-style teams, to invest in the initiatives that are of the highest priority to our customers and to the business at any given moment. And we can flex that up and down and side to side as our needs change.
We might, for an interval, be very focused on this part of the portfolio over here, and then we might be able to move to focusing on a different corner of the portfolio. No one has to get a new boss, and people can fluidly move from these things and get new opportunities to learn. It just strikes me as a much more appropriate organizational structure for our current stage.
You’re describing the shift from a divisional structure to a vastly more functional structure.
Everyone comes up, and there’s one big product meeting.
You obviously make a lot of software. I’ve described you as a software CEO. It seems like the software industry is in a moment of existential crisis about how software is made, about what a product manager versus an engineer versus a designer do. Are you still in the classic structures of building software? Or has AI completely upended what you’re doing?
No, we’re as deep in this as anyone. What’s been really fun for me over the course of the last year is to watch the software engineering team go from thoughtful skepticism to pretty deep embrace, if I’m honest. Some of that is on the back of just how dramatically the tools have evolved over the course of the last 12 months, certainly. 
I think almost everyone in the industry went home at the holidays at the tail end of 2025, coming into 2026, and came back just gobsmacked by how much progress the frontier labs were making on agentic coding, and it’s been a real accelerant for us. As complex as this transition is, I’m really excited about being able to help our engineers navigate what’s a pretty fundamental sea change in the way that this kind of infrastructure gets built, and it’s fun to get to be a part of that at this moment.
Did you break up the classic PM, designer, and engineer triad? Or is that still the core building block?
We still have all three, but it blurs particularly as the designers and the product managers can be prototypers at a really high level with incredible efficiency. It’s exciting to see how quickly they can communicate their ideas now in a medium that just didn’t exist at all for them a year ago.
We’re at the turn, right? You came in, you restructured the company, you identified a new thesis for the company. Today you’re here to talk about all the new news. Do you think you’re through it? Do you think the existing customers have forgiven you for the app mess? Do you think the brand has been restored?
Yeah, as we’ve been saying, I think that there’s the quant and there’s the qual. The quant is green across the board. Performance, reliability, customer care interactions, social tone, NPS — these things are all restored to levels that we enjoyed before any of that happened. 
On the qualitative side, I love the fact that I can show up on Reddit or on social media broadly and engage with our customers and have a constructive conversation about things that they’re excited that we’re doing, and things where we’re still disappointing an individual customer on some dimension.
I think that at some level, maybe this game is never over; you’re just always trying to polish off the remaining rough edges of everything that you do. So I have a real critic’s eye when I look at the work that we do, and if I ever let that slip, a customer will remind me of where the work remains. And so, yes, I think in every measurable way it’s behind us, but it’s a “never forget” chapter for the company.
That brings me to the other Decoder question: how do you make decisions? What’s your framework?
Well, I don’t think you bring just one framework to every decision. So we talk about, for example, product decisions. As an idea moves through its lifecycle from its days as an early little sapling that you have to care and tend to, through final mass production for a hardware object, and out into the channels, I think how you think about [each of those] decisions is different.
So in the earliest days, I really tried to protect the creativity of the company and to not let the antibodies of doubt and critique erode an idea before it’s had a chance to express itself in a way that anybody could get excited about. That means creating room for risk-taking, creativity, qualitative assessment, and prototyping before you get to the details of the business case and the hard trade-offs that you make on a journey from an idea to something you can actually ship.
But of course, as the programs roll along and they take on more and more financial investment and organizational risk, as more and more people aggregate into the product, you become, I think, just naturally much more quantitative in your analysis of the decisions. And you ask the teams to bring a really thoughtful, detailed description of the puts and takes and the risks associated with it, and you use that to help you make your decisions.
But maybe on top of all of that, you just have to hire great people. I mean, you just do, and you have to put them on teams that are an appropriate size for the task at hand. Tell me about the idea of naming the operating system Sonos 27. It’s obviously the middle of 2026. It obviously tracks Apple’s naming scheme. This very much implies there’ll be a Sonos 28 one year from now, in August of 2027. 
It does. I think from the beginning we knew that we wanted to give it a name, and we knew that we wanted the name to be able to express this idea that Sonos does evolve. And for many, many years, that evolution was to the great benefit of our customers. We had lossless audio for Apple. We had high-fidelity audio for Spotify. We had AirPlay. We had Alexa. 
Through the years, we’ve just over and over and over again expanded the capability of the products that were already in our customers’ homes, and we didn’t have a way of talking about it at all. So we wanted to give it a name. We wanted people to understand that it improved over time.
So as we started thinking about, “Well, how do you really do that?” I mean, the first thing they came to was like, “Gosh, we already have ‘OS’ right in the name of the company.” So to try to brand some entirely new thing felt like a self-own, and so we pretty quickly reverted to this idea that the product is 100 percent hardware and 100 percent software. The product is Sonos, not Arc. Maybe the OS2 is called Sonos.
And then it’s like, “Well, what companion moniker can we give it to drive that idea home?” Obviously we talked about version numbers and any number of other things, but we decided that we’d like to take advantage of this. Once a year, we’ll stand up in front of our audience and tell them about how the platform is evolving, and using the year as a descriptor for that was a better mechanism than almost anything else that was available to us.
Those software cycles, yearly big releases… Apple is basically the only company that sticks to it. Even if it doesn’t do it, it announces all the features, and then they slowly dribble them out over the course of the year as they come into focus. 
Again, I have a lot of questions about the nature of software development in 2027, but the idea that there’s one monolithic release once a year — the industry’s gotten away from that. Is that your idea, or are you going to do something different?
No, no, no. Fortunately, the industry has gotten away from that, and our intention is to have a moment where we can tell the story of the operating system roadmap for the next six or 10 months. As you’ll see, even in this moment, the things that we’re announcing — many of them will be available in what we’re calling early access, which is the chance for us to put them out into the product as opt-ins for our customers. Frankly, I think as we go into the event, we will talk about all of this. So to be able to say, “Look, part of what we’re communicating with the 27 of it all is that this stuff will come in 2027, and if it doesn’t, it’ll come in 2028 or beyond.”

I think sound is an incredible mood stabilizer, if you like. Take the audio track out of your favorite movie or television show, and so much of the life comes out of it. And I think having an out-loud audio experience in your home is something that everybody should enjoy. So part of the big picture is we want to spread this far and wide and make it accessible to everyone.
A running joke about the first generation of assistants is that they’ve ended up being for timers. And one of the new capabilities in Sonos 27 is our new voice assistant.
Our voice assistant is built on modern generative technology, but it’s really inspired by what people tell us that they like to see in the home. I’ll tell you, the killer app of the assistant is that they just want to be able to talk to it like a normal person, full stop. With the first-generation assistants, you just had to guess what to say every time, and even then maybe it took two or three attempts to get there. 
It’s such a game changer to be able to say, “Play that album I loved in college, the one with the Cocteau Twins singer. I think the song ended up as the theme song for that show. It was on Fox. It was about the curmudgeonly Doctor House… It’s ‘Teardrop’ by Massive Attack.”
I know. They took it off the [streaming version of House]. It’s sad.
It is. It is. So that’s job one, if you like. The first-generation assistants didn’t do it at all. Sonos Voice in the new OS is exceptional at this. So that’s meeting the customer where they are.
What else should they say? Well, they say a little bit about what I would call mood and ambiance. So lighting. Let’s bring lighting into the environment so that you can express a scene through both sound and light. 
My wife and I are constantly settling little bets in the kitchen: “What was this thing called? Who is that actor?” They do want comprehensive world knowledge. They want to get an answer to the kid’s homework assignment or whatever, and so these agents do need to be able to hand off to comprehensive frontier models to get perspectives on the world.
In some instances, those perspectives allow them to use the frontier model to manipulate the audio environment to play some music that people are talking about on TikTok and pick some stuff that sounds like the shoegaze music that I liked when I was in college. We can leverage the power of a frontier model to understand what’s being talked about on TikTok to sort that against my musical preferences, and deliver it.
I guess while we’re enumerating what I think a modern voice assistant has to do, it has to be fast, it has to be reliable, and it has to be responsible and affordable to run. I do think that customers want this as a fundamental capability of a product like Sonos, and we built an architecture that allows us to deliver it to every one of our customers as well.

That’s a pretty powerful building block as we see these OpenClaw-style agentic, proactive, asynchronous agents evolve. Now they have access to Sonos in a supportable way. So one thing that I’m reminded of in this moment is that we, as an industry, have these platform shifts that unlock opportunities for companies who get lucky on timing. For example, the original dot-com era was really powered by Oracle and Sun Solaris boxes and data centers that you owned and operated yourself. We then went through a chapter where the infrastructure became Linux and open source for your data tier. 
Of course, we’ve had this huge long run of cloud infrastructure. I think that if you’re a company that builds your stack on Solaris and Oracle, it’s really that there’s an opportunity for a company to come along and build a stack on Linux and Postgres in that moment and suddenly find efficiencies that are very, very hard for you to claim.
I think something very similar is happening in voice assistants. When I hear you talk on the show about your experience with voice assistants that are going through the transition from first generation to second generation, it feels to me like so much of the challenge there is about how we drag along all of the committed relationships that we have for the internet-connected toaster, back massager, and all of the things that are connected into those existing historical ecosystems. 
Honestly, even in the world of AI, with just how much has changed in the last couple of years underneath the companies as they’re building out their answers here, it really feels to me like we are stepping into a moment where agentic tool use powered by protocols, like MCP, is going to disintermediate a lot of that stuff that you’re talking about.
I think that in the immediate term, we’re really excited about what we can do in the use cases that our customers are telling us they care about. Give me mood and audio in the home. And I think we can take advantage of this shift to a truly next-generation architecture without the baggage of a decade of internet-connected light switches from 17 different protocols with 17 different hubs in the closet.
Well, I mean, part of the opportunity there is that you don’t have a big voice assistant. I don’t think the current Sonos voice assistant is at the scale of Alexa or Google Assistant. What are you going to do about the light switches that are already in the walls?

Just one last idea, since you said it a couple of times, this question about where the compute lives. I think that the answer to your questions, “Does this live in the cloud? Does this live in the home? Does this live in a box?” is yes. Just to make that really reductive, when I say “where is the computer” in the home context, what I mean is maybe in the ‘90s to early 2000s, there was a vision that we would all have home servers in our basements, and they would do all the logic of our home. They would have all the storage, and Microsoft would sell you a Windows home server in the basement and a Windows Media Center in the living room, and you and I probably both watched all of those Bill Gates keynotes at CES. 
None of that really ever came to pass. Instead, we put a lot of cheap computers near all the TVs, and they connected to cloud services, and they’re basically just running web browsers, as you well know. That is a very different version of what needed to happen and how the market played out.
In the smart home, I’ve got a bunch of automations in my house. When the garage is open, the lights turn on, and other stuff happens. At night, the doors all lock if they’re not locked. That logic has to live somewhere. My perspective on it is that it should live in my house. If the internet goes down, the lights should still turn on. 
This is not anything to do with big AI integrations or the new MCP way to address the Sonos system. Those are big ideas, and I’m just insistently dragging you back down into the dirt of: if the internet goes out, are the lights still going to turn on?
You don’t want to be the partner that puts in the internet-connected light switches that don’t work when the internet is down. 
But it’s not just the internet-connected light switches; it’s the logic of making it all work together.
I understand. Yeah, fair. Here’s what I’ll say about that. For 40 years now, we’ve been talking about technology for the home, starting with the personal computer, which is supposed to be the center of the technological household, but we didn’t really get that. We got laptops that people mostly use at work and use a bit at home.

So it’s super interesting. We’ll figure it out over time.
I feel like you’re this close to being like, “And then the Teslas will be a data center.” There’s something there that is maybe the line. Actually, I want to talk about that. I actually want to push on that a little bit. 
The initial Sonos innovation 100 years ago, when the company started, was, “Oh, we can build a mesh network. We can do wireless audio at scale. We can synchronize the latency of all the speakers so it sounds like the same music playing at the same time.” This was a lot of big engineering back in the day. 
Still, I mean, candidly, still. A lot of what our software team does day in and day out is extend and maintain that infrastructure.
There are features you’re announcing here as part of Sonos Fabric that I think are interesting. If you have surrounds, you can just place them, and they’ll figure out that they’re surrounds and immediately start being the surround speakers in a home theater. 
There’s just a lot of potential, as you’re describing, in the notion that, “Oh, there’s a big network of small computers in my house that can come together and do things you would not expect.” Is your focus that they will always do audio things? Or is it the focus that they will have many more capabilities?
I think any thoughtful product leader is going to tell you the focus is an important part of success. I do feel like there’s so much interesting work for us to do around creating an audio system that sets the mood for your home that I don’t want us to take our eye off of that opportunity. We are doing some really exciting things in Sonos Fabric and Sonos 27 that we should talk about, that get to some of the work that you’re describing.
But certainly in the moments where you allow yourself to think about what the company is in five years and what it will be in 10 years, you can’t help but interrogate what the opportunity is for a mesh — a fabric of compute that lives in the home.
I want to end by talking about headphones really quickly. We just had the CEO of Bose on. She and I had a pretty searching conversation about what happens to the headphone market in the time of AI wearables. 
My fear, my anxiety, about audio is always that consumers will always pick convenience over quality. It’s just the history of the... I’ve got a set of AirPods on this desk, and they don’t sound great, but boy, are they convenient. And that’s just the way it goes. It has always been what the market has demanded: convenience over quality.
We’re going to enter a time when Apple puts cameras on AirPods, and you can talk to them with Siri. When Google and Samsung ship very similar products, there’s undoubtedly going to be a flood of AI hardware startups that want to put something in your ears or in your body in some way. 
You are in the headphone market. You’re talking a lot about AI; you’re talking a lot about Fabric. That seems like a cataclysm coming for headphones. The same way that the removal of the headphone jack was a cataclysm in the headphone market, this seems like the next one. 
How are you preparing for that? Do you think there’s going to be a range of voice assistants on headphones, or do you think what you would call the first-party vendors are going to just grab more and more of that share?
Before we jump to the hypotheticals about where headphones are, can I tell you a little bit about the new headphones?
All right. So one of the things that you get from entering a new market is the opportunity to build something and put it in customers’ homes and learn a lot about what matters and what doesn’t matter.
So we launched Sonos Ace two years ago. I think measured against any of the other premium over-the-ear noise-canceling headphones in the market, they’re a great product. They’ve got great reviews; they have great noise cancelling. They’re super comfortable, and they look great. We’re really proud of the product, but they weren’t thoughtfully integrated into the Sonos ecosystem. 
I mean, at launch you could swap to one of our soundbars, not even all of our soundbars. I think it was the most visible expression of the missed opportunity of that moment for the company to always remember that the products that we make are part of the Sonos system, not individual offerings.
So we ended up with a great pair of headphones, but honestly, I mean, you review them all the time; there are lots of great headphones. When we set out to take all the lessons that we learned from Ace to design Ace Ultra, at the very top of that list is that we have to do the hard thing. These headphones have to be able to show up in your home as a part of the system, and the model through which you invoke your headphones has to be completely seamless and delightful.
We built an entirely new hardware platform for Ace Ultra called Headphone Engine 2, and it unlocks this capability at the hardware level. And then in Sonos OS 27, we built virtualization so that any one of the speakers in your home can deliver the audio platform to that speaker but can also act as a proxy for your headphones, which don’t have the horsepower to run the full stack — it would kill battery life, et cetera.
Now with Ace Ultra, you’ll be able to link your headphones to your Sonos system, walk up to a speaker that’s playing, press a button on your headphones, and the music will jump from the speaker into your headphones. No Bluetooth, no phone. You’ll be able to walk around your whole house, enjoy the music, come to another speaker, press the button again, and it will jump to that speaker using some BLA location-sensing stuff that we’ve developed. It’s super magical. It’s the one job that we had and didn’t deliver on with Ace. We’re really excited to get it out into the market.
Analogous to that on the home theater side is, as you mentioned, that we’re making all of our portable speakers — Sonos Play, Sonos Move — capable of being rear channels for home theater. That sounds really easy. Maybe people will even be like, “Why wasn’t that always possible?” But to your point about the deep technology of it, the way that we achieve high-fidelity, low-latency surround experiences in the living room is by directly bonding our rear channel speakers and subwoofer to the soundbar on a proprietary network, not through your access point. So for a speaker to seamlessly hop between being part of your Sonos system as a music node and part of your Sonos system as a surround channel means that you have to do a real-time reconfiguration of that networking stack, and you have to know when to do it.
We’re using accelerometers in the product to actually know that you’ve picked it up and set it down in a new location. We’re using Sonos’ positioning system, which is ultrasonic signaling, to broadcast to the room, “Hey, is there a soundbar here?” Ultrasonic comes back saying, “I’m here.” They negotiate position, left and right, and distance, so that they can optimize the surround sound experience. You pick it up again, you take it back to the kitchen, and it’s a regular speaker again. All happens magically, no use of the app. It’s pretty cool.
Answer my question on headphones, though. This is my big worry. You’ve got really cool headphones. They have a feature that no one else can ship, and Apple’s going to say, “Look, our new AirPods have Siri AI in them.” 
You can just say, “Show me what I’m looking at,” and a picture will be taken automatically and something will happen. We’ll get over the privacy implications of that, but that’s a collapse of the headphone market.
Maybe. I mean, headphones come in all kinds of form factors today: over-ear, in-ear, cuffs, wireless, wired. So I do think it’s a market where people choose different form factors for different tasks. We’re really focused on this personal in-the-home listening — what do you do when the baby’s asleep? What do you do when you want to move the party from the kitchen to the den while you relax for the evening? We think that there’s a bunch of really interesting use cases there that other people aren’t paying attention to.
I think, broadly, over the course of the next couple of years, we’re going to get all kinds of adventurous wackadoodle consumer electronics that are connected to this new emerging AI universe. Most of them will be a swing and a miss. Of course, we’ve already seen some of those. So it’s a little hard to speculate, I think, about which of these things, if any, is going to have its iPod moment or its iPhone moment or whatever.
What do you think is going to happen?
I think we’re going to see a replay of what happened when the headphone jack got taken away. The headphone jack was an open interconnect. There was a really vibrant market for all kinds of headphones, and a bunch of those companies don’t exist anymore. The high-end wired headphones, for phones anyway, have mostly gone away, and you have a bunch of medium Bluetooth competitors, but the phone makers have largely taken that with first-party products. 
Now, you have your products at the high end competing with really high-end noise-canceling products from Bose and Sony and whoever, and that is the airplane set. The lack of the open interconnect has really killed the vibrancy of the low and middle end of the market.
Okay, well, there’s one big thing they can do to make sure the high end belongs to them, and it’s to integrate AI in very specific ways directly into their operating system. We’ll see how that plays out. There’s also a thing that’s different this time: there’s a vastly more energized European regulatory environment. Who knows how this will play out?
I can’t tell you, but all that stuff is a swirl, and you’re a headphone maker, and it seems like different headphone makers are taking different approaches to this.
The only counter that I might offer is that there’s a lot of talk about the walled garden of the Bluetooth advantages that the platform companies have. But I would say even without the European regulators, it’s notable that something like the Meta Glasses can have a reasonable, I think, commercially viable set of experiences that are principally powered by compute that lives on your phone and still deliver conversational AI that is mediated by a Bluetooth connection, admittedly behind some of the obstacles that you’re describing. But those obstacles aren’t so profound that clever companies aren’t figuring out how to work within those constraints.
I’m very curious to see how that plays out. It doesn’t seem like it’s in focus. Again, probably because, as you say, none of the products are in focus. No one knows what a hit product here looks like, so you might as well let a thousand flowers bloom and then radically constrict the market.
Tom, I’ve burned just a ton of your time. I think you can tell I could talk to you for ages and ages about all kinds of things.
Tell us what’s next for Sonos. When does all this stuff ship?
So I think by the time this airs, we’ll have announced all of this to the world. We’re having a big event in New York to share Sonos OS 27, Sonos Voice 27, and the Ace Ultra and Beam Ultra. We can’t wait to get this stuff out into the world and begin to hear what our customers do with all of these exciting new products.
Many of the software features are going to be available in early access, which will mean our customers will opt into them, be able to give us feedback, and we’ll be able to observe the telemetry that comes back from their homes and make sure that we’re delivering exactly the experience that we want. We’re excited about the moment of co-creation that’s around the corner for us.
As we talked about at the top of the hour, Sonos 27 is absolutely a nod to the fact that we intend to keep doing this until the sun burns out. There’ll be Sonos 28 and 29 and 30 and beyond.
That’s great. All right, I’ve got to ask you at the end: I have ceiling speakers in my kitchen. They’re connected to a Sonos Amp. There’s a Google Home Hub right there, and it’s broken. I can’t ask it to play music in the kitchen. When are you going to fix that for me? I’m ending on tech support.
All right. I don’t know the answer, but I’d love to figure it out for you. I know the right folks to call, so let’s get you connected.
We’re going to have a Decoder roundtable.
If your listeners have similar kinds of problems, we’ve got great people to help them, and we always like to hear from you. You can find me on social pretty easily.
Usually I end by inviting people back, but I’m saying we’ve got to fix it, and then we’re going to talk about what it took to fix it. That’s the plan.
Tom, this is great. Thank you so much, man.
This was super fun. Thank you.
Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!
