articles.body:
Someone opened a PR to implement readahead in Turso. It was a throwaway implementation, but a good excuse to measure io_uring and understand more about it.
Turso has two backends. syscall uses pread(2). io_uring uses io_uring, and opens the database file with O_DIRECT with no option to use buffered I/O. O_DIRECT takes away kernel readahead, so getting it back means implementing it in the application.1
The PR’s results are impressive. io_uring with an application buffer is faster. I want to understand why.
Without readahead, io_uring issues only one entry at a time. The problem is the lack of concurrency: each read waits for the previous one. The application knows that “hey, at this time, I need page 100”, which means: Turso submits a read SQE for page 100, then waits for it. The scan continues. Now Turso needs page 101, so it submits a new read SQE that page.
With readahead on, things change. Turso needs page 100, detects sequential access, and instead of asking for one page it submits reads for pages 100 through 131. Now 32 reads are in flight at the same time.
The measurements below use TPC-H, a standard benchmark for analytic databases, on a 1.2 GiB database.
Q6, the query I measured, does a full scan on lineitem, the biggest table of the benchmark.
off means PRAGMA prefetch_pages=0: The PR’s code without readahead.
on means a window of 32 pages.
I wanted to see what readahead changes in the I/O path: how many requests Turso submits, and what arrives at the device. So I ran iostat -dxm 1 sda alongside Q6, and perf stat counting the io_uring:io_uring_submit_req tracepoint.
rareq-sz is the average size of a read request arriving at the device. %rrqm is the percentage of read requests merged with another request before being issued.
With readahead on, Turso emits 23,005 more SQEs, and it fetches more pages than needed, making the device read more bytes. But the device receives fewer requests.
If two requests in the queue cover sectors that are next to each other, the block layer joins them into one bigger request. This only works if both requests are in the queue at the same time. I counted the merge tracepoints with perf.
With readahead off, only 140 of 195,516 bios merged. It makes sense since there’s only one SQE in the queue and there’s nothing to merge. With readahead on, 202,539 of 218,493 bios merged, and the device received only 15,951 requests. Since there were multiple SQEs in the queue, the kernel merged them.
Turso uses io_uring with sqpoll. The sqpoll uses a thread that spins checking if work was delivered and if the kernel should do something. It’s a thread that keeps track of work, at the cost of spinning.
I timed the execution of sqpoll with prefetch_pages=32 to see where the time was being spent: 8.22s of wall time, 3.70s of user time and 8.46s of system time (median of seven runs). The system time is bigger than wall time, and this is only possible when two threads spend CPU at the same time.
I expected the cycles to be in the query code, but:
Q6 on the io_uring backend with SQ polling. io_sq_thread, the kernel polling thread, is at 65% of cycles.
So I rebuilt Turso without SQ polling, replacing the setup_sqpoll builder with the plain IoUring::new, which is already Turso’s fallback when sqpoll setup fails.
Plain/default ring: 8.62s of wall, 3.62s of user, and 1.27s of system time. Removing the polling thread made wall time a little worse and the system time much smaller. The system time isn’t zero because we are still calling io_uring_enter(2) per submission, and Turso submits one SQE at a time.
If polling is worth it or not depends on the machine. Didona et al. measured this in a 2022 SYSTOR paper: submission polling with one NVMe drive and one CPU core reached only 13 KIOPS (13 thousand IO operations per second) - the two threads had to share one core, so they took turns. With a second core, performance completely recovered. This box I’m using has 4 vCPUs. The query is single-threaded and uses one ring with one polling thread, and there was always a free core for the polling thread, so it never competed for CPU with the queries.
With SQ polling off, I timed Q6 again on both backends: 8.55s on io_uring and 3.02s on syscall. The difference is significant. I want to understand where that extra time goes, so I counted instructions and cache misses with perf. One note about the counters in this table: they come from a rebuilt host (who wants to pay Hetzner for idle time?), so their absolute values don’t match the timings above.
io_uring runs 0.2 B more instructions which is almost nothing, but it takes 4.8 M more cache misses.
Both backends use DMA: the disk hardware writes the data into RAM by itself, without the CPU doing the work. But there are differences between the two backends as well: in a buffered read, the disk writes the data into the page cache.2 Then the kernel copies the data from the page cache into the process buffer. This copy is normal CPU work: the CPU reads bytes and writes them somewhere. A side effect of copy: the data ends up in the CPU caches (L1/L2/L3).
With O_DIRECT, though, the disk writes the data into the process buffer directly without the copy step, which means the CPU doesn’t get involved in the process, so nothing is copied to the CPU caches.
This explanation is a hypothesis, the counters show that io_uring has more cache misses than syscall, but I never traced the misses back to the missing copy step.
After all of this, I have some opinions about the cost of each model:
io_uring with O_DIRECT and without readahead on the application side runs with a single SQE in the ring. One SQE means no concurrency, and without concurrency the block layer has nothing to merge. This was the slowest configuration in my measurements.
sqpoll is a reasonable model when the machine has more than one vCPU. But you still need to understand how your application uses resources. If the application is already CPU heavy, the polling thread will compete with it for CPU. In that case, it’s a good idea to measure the impact of dedicating one vCPU to the kernel thread before turning sqpoll on.
plain/default io_uring is also reasonable, because it can batch. Only one io_uring_enter(2) batches multiple SQEs. The SYSTOR paper measured this: 1.01 syscalls per I/O at queue depth 64. Turso does not batch today, so it pays one syscall per page. The submission loop already calls submit_and_wait for all pending operations, but the pager asks for one page and waits for it, so there’s never more than one operation pending:
Besides the models, two other things about cost:
In a buffered read, the kernel copies the data from the page cache to the process buffer, and this copy uses the CPU. The copy has a side effect: the data ends up warm in the CPU caches. O_DIRECT skips the copy, but the data still has to reach the CPU at some point. In the buffered read, that happens during the copy. With O_DIRECT, it happens during the query, as cache misses.
Readahead wastes some work. Turso submitted 23,005 more SQEs, fetched pages the query never used, and the device read more bytes. But the extra requests keep the queue full, without them, the queue would go back to holding one request at a time.

articles.body:
Florida is banning Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers across state highways, as reported earlier by NBC News and local news outlet WUSF. In a memo on Monday, Florida’s Department of Transportation says it’s revoking permits for all license plate readers, adding that they must be removed from state highways within 30 days.
As noted in the memo, Florida’s DOT says it’s issuing the order in response to the “recent exponential increase in deployments” of license plate readers, “coupled with concerning reports of misuse, data privacy concerns, and surveillance schemes.” The agency is also halting future requests for license plate reader placements on state roadways.
The move comes about a week after Florida Governor Ron DeSantis acknowledged concerns about Flock cameras and license plate readers, saying they’re “out of control. Last month, Texas Governor Greg Abbott froze state spending on Flock cameras as backlash surrounding the cameras grows. Several communities, including Lansing, Michigan; Tempe, Arizona; and Knox County, Tennessee, have ended Flock camera contracts as well.

articles.title: Barcelona complete signing of Arsenal striker Jesus
articles.summary: Barcelona have completed the signing of Gabriel Jesus on a permanent deal.
articles.body: Barcelona have completed the signing of Gabriel Jesus on a permanent deal. It comes after BBC Sport reported that a deal for the Brazilian to move to Barcelona for a fee of £8.6m (10m euros) was close to be being confirmed.Jesus has fallen down the pecking order in recent seasons at Arsenal due to injury issues, as well as Kai Havertz and Viktor Gyokeres being the preferred central strikers at the club. Napoli had also shown an interest in Jesus, but the Brazilian has now joined last season's Spanish league champions after completing his medical on Monday. Jesus joined Arsenal from Manchester City in 2022, scoring 32 goals and adding 22 assists in 123 appearances for the Gunners.Speaking to the media before Arsenal's win over Aston Villa, Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta confirmed that Jesus was not training with the squad. When asked whether that meant the forward was leaving, Arteta said: "Personal situations, whatever they are, I think it's clear."Jesus would be Barcelona's third signing from a Premier League club this summer, following the arrivals of Anthony Gordon from Newcastle and Rodri from Manchester City.Barcelona have also been pursuing a deal for Atletico Madrid striker Julian Alvarez but Atletico have been clear of their intention to not negotiate with their La Liga rivals. Arsenal have also been chasing Alvarez but it is unlikely that a deal is completed at this stage.The Gunners have also sold Fabio Vieira to Hamburger SV while Ethan Nwaneri is getting closer to completing a loan move to Borussia Dortmund.

articles.title: BBC's Ski Sunday to end after nearly 50 years
articles.summary: The BBC is to end its Ski Sunday programme after nearly 50 years.
articles.body: Ski Sunday, the BBC's winter sports programme, is to end after nearly 50 years.First broadcast in 1978, it featured the best of winter sports action, with Ed Leigh and Chemmy Alcott its most recent presenting team."Changing audience behaviours and the tough financial decisions needed to meet savings requirements mean BBC Sport must continually review how it delivers value for licence fee payers and serves audiences across all platforms. This decision forms part of that process," said a BBC Sport statement.Philip Bernie, head of BBC Sport events, said Ski Sunday "has been a truly iconic programme".He added: "Generations of viewers have enjoyed its coverage of the best in winter sports. "We are enormously proud of the role it has played in bringing these moments to audiences across the UK, and extremely grateful to the brilliant people who have delivered them, not least the current outstanding team."These decisions are never easy, but as audience viewing habits evolve and we work to deliver value for licence fee payers, we have to make tough choices. "We remain committed to bringing audiences the very best of winter sport, above all at the Winter Olympics, across BBC Sport's platforms."

articles.title: Get ready for a really busy month of smartphones
articles.summary:
At what point are there simply too many phones? | Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge

articles.body:
We’re not even half a day into September, and two new smartphones have already launched: the Poco F9 Pro and F9 Ultra. We’re expecting more this week, as the IFA trade show kicks off in Berlin, before we get new iPhones a week after that. And that’s only the beginning of what promises to be an exceptionally busy month for smartphone launches.
For the decade I’ve worked in the industry, tech journalists have always spoken in hushed tones about the dreaded “Techtember,” when just about every tech company on the planet seems to be in unspoken agreement that it’s time to launch new products in time for the holiday buying season. (It’s followed, in particularly packed years, by Techtober too). In the last few years the pressure has lessened a little, the release calendar stretching out into neighboring months. But in 2026 Techtember is back with a vengeance, especially when it comes to phones.
It always starts with IFA. Europe’s biggest tech trade show attracts over 200,000 visitors and global manufacturers from across tech. IFA doesn’t have as many phone launches as it did a decade ago, when the likes of Sony, Samsung, and LG would routinely launch flagships at the show, but there’s still plenty on the way this week. 
Tecno has teased a bezelless concept phone, which it says it’ll be bringing to the show. TCL usually brings an array of E Ink-esque Nxtpaper phones to show, so I’d hope to see some at its press conference. There’s even an outside chance of a whole new foldable: Xiaomi is attending IFA for the first time ever, just a week after it teased the upcoming Xiaomi 18 Fold and promised the phone a launch in early September. Its September 3rd press conference would certainly make sense for that.
Then there’s Apple. The company won’t be at IFA, but it has already announced a September 9th event, where we expect it to launch new iPhones. Rumor has it that it’s splitting its launch up in an act of solidarity with overworked phone reviewers (I wish), delaying the regular iPhone 18 to next spring and sticking to the Pros this month. Still, the long-awaited arrival of the first foldable iPhone should be enough to keep us busy.
But that’s far from all that’s coming. Android Headlines reckons at least 20 phones will launch this month, and that might be a conservative estimate. 
Huawei will launch its latest trifold, the Mate XT 2, in China on September 7th, and perhaps the Mate 90 lineup too. Xiaomi will follow up the 18 Fold with the 18 Pro lineup later in the month. Vivo has confirmed its flagship X500 series will also arrive in September, and Honor has done the same for its Magic 9 flagships. Oppo’s Find X10 line has been heavily tipped to arrive in September too, though thankfully some suggest it might slip to the following month. Even OnePlus is expected to get in on the action: its OnePlus 16 rumored to release in September too — though not in the US or Europe.
Why the sudden glut? I blame Qualcomm. It used to launch its flagship Snapdragon chips in December, but that launch date has steadily moved forward, in part to give manufacturers time to ship new products ahead of lucrative holiday sales seasons, both in China and abroad. So this year it’s holding its annual Snapdragon Summit from September 22nd to 24th, when it’s likely to reveal the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6. Promptly after that, we can expect a rush of Android manufacturers announcing phones powered by the new silicon.
With RAMageddon in full swing, the jury’s still out on how appealing these launches will be. Outside of Samsung’s fun Galaxy Z Fold 8, a lot of this year’s biggest phones have been rehashes of 2025 models with a price hike and a chipset bump — and occasionally not even that. At least we’ll have more foldables to be excited about, and hopefully a couple of manufacturers have another surprise or two in store.
A month chock-full of phones, that I can do. But if we’re about to get a Techtember full of iterative updates that cost more, without delivering anything special? Wake me up when it’s Techtober.

articles.title: Nvidia’s controversial DLSS 5 arrives September 3rd and requires serious GPU horsepower
articles.summary: Nvidia is officially launching DLSS 5 this week, following a divisive announcement in March where we likened the AI upscaling tech to a "real-time generative AI filter for video games" and "motion smoothing for video games, but worse." articles.body:
Nvidia is officially launching DLSS 5 this week, following a divisive announcement in March where we likened the AI upscaling tech to a “real-time generative AI filter for video games” and “motion smoothing for video games, but worse.” DLSS 5 will officially be available on RTX 50-series desktop and laptop GPUs and through GeForce Now cloud gaming, though the only game with the tech so far is NBA 2K27 — which is launching September 3rd at 9PM PT on PC.
When it was announced, Nvidia lauded DLSS 5 as “the company’s most significant breakthrough in computer graphics since the debut of real-time ray tracing in 2018,” and highlighted how the tech uses AI to make games look more realistic by enhancing a game based on its source content. Nvidia also stressed that DLSS 5 gave developers controls that let them decide how changes from DLSS 5 appeared in their games.
Image compare: drag the handle to see the difference Nvidia says it can provide in NBA 2K27. Tap here for full-res with DLSS 5 off, and with DLSS 5 on.
But accompanying examples shared by Nvidia were widely criticized and meme’d on for significantly changing how characters looked, such as the “yassification” of Resident Evil Requiem protagonist Grace Ashcroft. With the official launch, Requiem still doesn’t support DLSS 5, and neither do other games shown in the March reveal, including EA Sports FC, Starfield, and Hogwarts Legacy, so we don’t know how the final version of the tech might now appear in those titles.
Nvidia did not answer our questions about when DLSS 5 might come to any game beyond NBA 2K27, nor reconfirm that previously confirmed titles will still include the tech.
[Image: Tap, twice, for higher res versions. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/assets_2026_08_1788195652_nba-2k27-nvidia-dlss-5-comparison-002-off.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: Tap, twice, for higher res versions. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/assets_2026_08_1788195652_nba-2k27-nvidia-dlss-5-comparison-002-on.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
In examples from NBA 2K27 we saw in a press briefing, though, changes from DLSS 5 don’t appear to be quite as dramatic as the types of adjustments shown in the initial reveal. The shadows and textures added by DLSS 5 generally made the players in the game look more realistic instead of turning them into AI caricatures. You can see more in our deeper dive here.
In briefings, Nvidia showed how developers will have many sliders at their disposal to determine exactly how much DLSS 5 changes things, and that developers can choose to amp up whichever parts of the scene they prefer. They can even leave characters’ faces alone and just enhance silverware or food or foliage, Nvidia says.
Image slider: drag the handle to make bacon look more real by giving it shadows.
While Nvidia’s original DLSS 5 demos required a pair of RTX 5090 gaming graphics cards, the company claims even a single midrange RTX 5060 can manage to play NBA 2K27 at 1080p with ray tracing and DLSS 5 at ultra spec — if you have one of he fastest gaming CPUs and enable 6x frame generation (meaning the game is only producing one “real” frame for every six frames you see).
DLSS 5 is still a huge performance hit. Nvidia estimates it at 50 to 60 percent, and we saw performance cut in half when we tried an unofficial DLSS5 mod in Shadow of the Tomb Raider.
So far, Nvidia has shown us examples that demonstrate the ideal version of what’s possible with DLSS 5 (and promote NBA 2K27). We haven’t yet tested an official build of DLSS 5 ourselves to get an idea of how the tech might look, but we have tried the unofficial version that modders are using to mess with older games like Control and Skyrim. With older games, it seems, a little sprinkle of DLSS 5 goes a long way.

articles.title: Nvidia’s DLSS 5, explained
articles.summary:
Lara Croft in Shadow of the Tomb Raider, with a  DLSS 5 mod applied. | Screenshot by Sean Hollister / The Verge	

Nvidia knows that DLSS 5 left a bad first impression. In March, many gamers took one look at Resident Evil Requiem protagonist Grace Ashcroft's DLSS 5-ified face and declared it AI slop. So this week, the company's re-introducing its controversial "neural rendering" with firm messaging
articles.body:
Nvidia knows that DLSS 5 left a bad first impression. In March, many gamers took one look at Resident Evil Requiem protagonist Grace Ashcroft’s DLSS 5-ified face and declared it AI slop. So this week, the company’s re-introducing its controversial “neural rendering” with firm messaging about how it “preserves artistic intent,” “respects the rendered frame,” and gives game developers full control.
Now, ahead of its September 3rd launch, with an official Nvidia briefing under our belt and some hands-on time with the version that leaked onto the web, we think we finally get the picture. Here’s what’s going on.
Is DLSS 5 AI slop?
The critics weren’t wrong: DLSS 5 largely is a generative AI filter for video games. Kind of like a camera filter on your phone, DLSS 5 analyzes and modifies a real-time stream of 2D images after your 3D game engine is done spitting them out. It can indeed make game characters look terrible if applied poorly, like they’ve aged 20 years in a split-second. It uses a lot of GPU power, and can easily cut framerate in half — even applied well, you could argue that existing games look better without it.
But DLSS 5 isn’t what we typically think of when we think of generative AI. It doesn’t change shapes, or hallucinate words on a sign, or place brand-new fake objects in view. Instead, it imagines light, shadow, color, and detail that make the same shapes appear differently.
DLSS 5 can make dull, pasty characters look far more photorealistic. It can fill their hair and clothing and nearby foliage with signs of realistic light. It can ground characters and objects and clothing so they don’t look like they’re floating above video game surfaces.
Here’s an example I captured myself in Yakuza Kiwami: with DLSS on, see how contact shadows underneath each character make them seem like they’re actually standing on the ground?
(Later in this story, you should really check out how Cade Cunningham’s jersey casts shadows on his video game body, so it looks more like he’s wearing it.)
And unlike AI-generated photos and videos, that usually produce different results with the same prompt, Nvidia claims DLSS 5 is deterministic, so games should look the same every time.
DLSS 5 is also not one-size-fits-all. Despite what it sounds like, “DLSS 5 On” and “DLSS 5 Off” isn’t just an on-off switch. Developers (and apparently modders) can drag various sliders to change how DLSS 5 plays with color and light, and they have three different AI models to work with at launch, giving your graphics “default,” “natural” or “cinematic” looks.
Plus, developers can decide whether to apply DLSS 5 to everything in a scene, just a character’s face and skin, just foliage, just silverware or furniture or even just food.
You’re saying game studios could leave character faces alone?
Yep. The toolset can automatically cut out a mask, like in Photoshop, to isolate a character’s face and skin from everything else:
[Image: The automated mask precisely selects this character’s face, so game developers can enhance it — or make sure it’s left alone. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/nvidia-dlss-5-010.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
If they don’t like the automated mask, devs can cut one out themselves. That’s the little “Developer Masking” checkbox in the image above. “There’s no limit to how many masks, how many groups, they could implement,” says Nvidia’s director of real-time content technology Gabriele Leone.
Would game studios actually leave the faces alone?
Probably not! The first game brave enough to ship with the tech is NBA 2K27, and I suspect that’s because Cade Cunningham actually looks a bit better with detailed skin, a uniform that doesn’t seem glued to his body, and a bit more glint in his eye. Take a look at Nvidia’s images for yourself:
That basketball, too — doesn’t it feel a bit more lifelike now most of its detail is in shadow?
But what about DLSStelle and all the other horrific AI faces I’ve seen since modders got hold of the tech?
Truly deranged. But these games are supposed to look like animation, and surely their creators would never do anything like this to them, right? Right??
“The soul and goal of GeForce is to achieve photorealism in real-time rendering,” Nvidia’s director of applied deep learning Edward Liu told journalists. And games with more realistic art styles don’t look anywhere near this bad. But even realistic games can look wrong if the sliders are set too aggressively.
What do you mean by “too aggressively?”
I’m willing to bet that if you’ve seen the leaked DLSS 5 modifying an existing game, the unofficial DLSS 5 mod was set to its default level of around 80 percent intensity or even higher. Some creators will even pump it up to 200 percent to make the difference between “DLSS on” and “DLSS off” especially clear.
But I believe even 80 percent is far too aggressive for many existing games. It can feel like you’re artificially aging a character by weathering their skin and deepening the wrinkles and creases in their face.
To show you, I fired up Shadow of the Tomb Raider. Here’s what Lara Croft looks like with DLSS 5 at 0 percent, 80 percent, and 200 percent intensity:
She seems… weathered, no? But at 40 percent intensity, she still looks like the same video game character to me, only with a bit more life in her eyes:
Similarly, here’s Kazuma Kiryu from Yakuza Kiwami once more. In this part of the game, he’s supposed to be 27 years old, and nowhere near the grizzled veteran he is by Yakuza 6. But as I ramp up the intensity from 0 to 40 to 85 percent, you can see his furrowed brow gets more furrowed, his hair lightens, and the increased shadow across his cheeks makes his face appear slightly gaunt.
He looks older — even if the underlying geometry of his face hasn’t actually changed. In a cutscene at 85 percent, it even looks like his hair might be tinged with grey:
[Image: Does this look like a 27-year-old man to you? https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/YakuzaKiwami-2026-08-31-00-15-21_57.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
But again, it’s something developers and modders can control with some granularity. I’d probably enjoy a version of DLSS 5 for older games that ignores the faces but enhances a character’s gear. Kiryu’s sworn brother and antagonist Majima, below, doesn’t quite look right to me — but his eyepatch and necklace look excellent.
By the way, these are just me playing with the overarching DLSS 5 slider when set to its “default” model. There are actually three different AI models, each with a slightly different look, and two different sliders, one for “tone” and one for “structure.”
I’m telling myself that “tone” is about light and color, while “structure” is about shadows and definition. But it’s probably easier to show you by isolating each:
Officially, Nvidia says that “structure intensity” controls a mix of ambient occlusion, contact shadows, reflections and subsurface scattering (read: how light scatters through materials like hair, skin, and leaves), while “tone intensity” controls color and “broader lighting” details.
What about the three different AI models?
Nvidia only called them Model A, Model B and Model C in my briefing, but the DLSS 5 mod I used describes them as “default,” “cinematic” and “natural.” Here’s the image Nvidia provided to show the difference:
[Image: Nvidia’s three AI looks. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/nvidia-dlss-5-012.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
And here’s my own comparison in Shadow of the Tomb Raider — you may need to blow these up and cycle through to spot the differences.
Is this really an AI filter? It doesn’t use the game engine at all?
Nvidia says that DLSS 5 can take some cues from game engines. But it’s based on the colors and motion vectors that it sees in the flat 2D frames, after they’re rendered and after other techniques like DLSS Super Resolution are applied.
When we asked how DLSS 5 knows the difference between a character model, an object, and a piece of foliage, Liu replied that the model was trained to recognize what it sees. “Just like a person, if you look at anything, you know where things are.”
You can even technically run DLSS 5 on video capture from a Nintendo Switch 2, and modders have already found ways to inject it into earlier games that used OpenGL and DirectX 9.
Will game developers actually buy into DLSS 5? Will they use it well?
That’s one of the big remaining questions — and one that Nvidia left unanswered during and after our briefing.
While Nvidia said in March that DLSS 5 would come to at least 16 different games including Assassin’s Creed Shadows, Hogwarts Legacy, Starfield, and Resident Evil Requiem, the company did not answer questions about when DLSS 5 might come to any game beyond NBA 2K27, nor did it confirm that other titles are still coming following the original backlash. Perhaps Nvidia and its partners will wait and see how reviewers and gamers react first.
It’s worth noting that this may be a niche technology to start: while it no longer requires two RTX 5090 GPUs to function, it still uses a lot of horsepower. Officially, DLSS 5 is only coming to the latest RTX 50 series GPUs, which have become quite expensive: even a lower-mid-range RTX 5060 retailers for around $470 these days.
Nvidia claims that an RTX 5060 is enough to play NBA 2K27 at 1080p with ultra settings, ray tracing, and DLSS 5 enabled — assuming you’re pairing it with a fast gaming CPU and a whole heap of RAM.
[Image: These framerates are with 6x frame-gen enabled, so divide by six to get a better idea of how responsive the game might feel. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/nvidia-dlss-5-018.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Just how much of a performance hit are we talking?
With NBA 2K27, Nvidia claims the performance hit is 50 to 60 percent on average across all Nvidia RTX 50-series GPUs. When I ran the Shadow of the Tomb Raider benchmark at 1440p with on an RTX 5090 at Highest spec, DLSS Quality and an unofficial DLSS 5 mod, I saw framerate exactly cut in half — 312fps with DLSS 5 off, 156fps with it on.
Will gamers be able to tweak DLSS 5 the way they like?
The DLSS 5 mods are so easy to apply, it seems like the cat is out of the bag. But Nvidia’s message is that the developer has full control, and it didn’t answer questions about whether it’ll provide controls to gamers, too.
Which mod should I install?
I don’t yet feel comfortable recommending one — there’s been a feeding frenzy for DLSS 5 mods ever since the leak and we haven’t been able to properly vet. I installed one on a completely fresh system, just in case something went wrong.
How have gamers reacted to Nvidia’s re-introduction of DLSS 5 so far?
The reactions have been all over the place since DLSS 5 leaked and modders began posting their work. I’ve seen people say that DLSS 5 looks like a free next-gen remaster of any game you like, and I’ve seen people say it looks as terrible as it did before. I’ve seen people suggest that even if it looks good, it’ll make every game look too similar once developers start using it as a crutch.
But many of those impressions were based on images and videos of the tech at its extremes. Once people realize there’s granular control, perhaps reactions will become more measured.
Correction: An earlier version of this article misidentified characters in screenshots; they are NBA player Cade Cunningham and Majima from Yakuza.

articles.title: Roku’s first OLED TVs undercut the midrange competition
articles.summary:
The Roku Pro Series OLED TV. | Image: Roku	

Just a few weeks ago the only midrange OLED options available were from LG and Samsung. But after Sony officially announced the Bravia 6 last week, Roku has now launched its first-ever OLED TV - the Roku Pro Series - which will be followed by the step-up Pro Series LX next month.
The Roku Pro Series has a 120Hz panel, four HDMI 2.1 ports, and supports D
articles.body:
Just a few weeks ago the only midrange OLED options available were from LG and Samsung. But after Sony officially announced the Bravia 6 last week, Roku has now launched its first-ever OLED TV — the Roku Pro Series — which will be followed by the step-up Pro Series LX next month.
The Roku Pro Series has a 120Hz panel, four HDMI 2.1 ports, and supports Dolby Vision and HDR10 Plus. It also has auto low latency mode, FreeSync Premium, and VRR for gaming. A backlit Roku remote is included, and a remote finder button on the TV helps locate it when misplaced. The Pro Series LX is about twice as bright as the regular Pro Series, supports 144Hz VRR, and has a polarizer to reduce reflections. And of course both TV series use the Roku operating system.
The Pro Series is exclusive to Amazon for 2026, available now, and comes in 55- and 65-inch sizes starting at $999. The Pro Series LX will be available in October in 55 inches for $1,299 and 65 inches for $1,599.

articles.body:
Mozilla is officially launching ad blocking for Firefox on iOS today, after testing the feature over the past few weeks. The new built-in option will block most third-party ads and trackers before they load on an iPhone, reducing bandwidth use and decluttering mobile websites.
Mozilla is using Apple’s WebKit Content Blocker technology and the EasyList filter to block ads in Firefox on iOS, so you won’t need to download and install a separate extension to get it working. The ad blocking is controlled in the settings of Firefox on iOS, and Mozilla is keeping it disabled by default so you have to enable it from settings > browsing > ad blocker. You can also toggle it on or off during a browsing session from the site menu option.
While this is the first time Firefox has gained ad blocking support on iOS, there are plenty of rival browsers that already offer similar support. Brave, Vivaldi, Opera, and others also have built-in ad blockers on iOS.
