articles.title: The final minutes before floodwater crashed through Nepal-China border
articles.summary: More than 100 Indians are missing at a vital Nepal-China trade crossing after devastating Himalayan floods.
articles.body: The video lasts only seconds.A dark wall appears from behind the buildings at Gyirong, on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border. At first, it looks almost like a black cloud. Then it gathers shape and speed: water, mud, boulders, ice and rock surging down the valley. The CCTV footage, whose timestamp reads 10:59:53, went viral.For many, it was the first visual evidence of the sheer scale of the destruction that was unfolding.What happened in the minutes that followed is still difficult to reconstruct. But fragments of video and satellite imagery show much of the border complex swept away, with buildings that once crowded the valley floor simply gone.Electronic immigration records from Nepal's Rasuwagadhi border post are filling some gaps, as well as insights from its only surviving staff member. Tika Ram Pokharel, who happened to be in Kathmandu sitting an exam on the day, tells the BBC the crossing was unusually busy when floodwater hit."This is a historic travel route between Kathmandu and Tibet," explains Kathmandu-based hydrologist Ajay Dixit. "The area is geologically vulnerable, characterised by deep gorges and steep rivers that flow at high velocity, carry heavy sediment and can bring down huge boulders."It is a place where pilgrims heading towards Mount Kailash cross paths with traders travelling between Nepal and China, truck drivers, customs officials, tourists and people who live along the border.On the morning of the flood, more than 100 Indians may have been in or around the crossing. At least 275 Indians remain missing in Nepal, according to India's foreign ministry.Nepal's immigration department has been trying to reconstruct who passed through Rasuwagadhi in the final hours before the disaster.Electronic records show that 89 Nepali and foreign nationals had cleared immigration to leave Nepal for Tibet, while four people had registered their entry into Nepal.The immigration system recorded its final transaction at 08:35:03 local time (10:52 Tibet time), less than 10 minutes before the torrent appeared on the CCTV footage at Gyirong.Four immigration employees, including the head of the Rasuwagadhi office, went missing in the floods. His body was later recovered far downstream. The female official who recorded the final transactions is still missing.Among the foreign nationals recorded leaving Nepal that morning were 32 Indians, 12 Chinese nationals and nine Americans, as well as citizens of Britain, Canada, Australia and Italy.Tika Ram Pokharel, the surviving senior immigration assistant at Rasuwagadhi, says the electronic records capture only part of what was happening at the border that morning.The immigration office stood at Ghatte Khola Bazar, about 1.5km north of Timure, a small trading settlement clustered around the crossing. From there, it was another 2km to the Friendship Bridge marking the border with Tibet. Along that stretch were shops, hotels and parking areas where travellers and vehicles gathered before crossing.The Nepalese immigration office opened at 08:00, Pokharel says. Once travellers had cleared immigration, they could continue towards the border or wait in the area before crossing.When Pokharel called a colleague at 08:20 that morning, he was told the crossing was unusually busy. Around 300 to 400 people were waiting to leave Nepal for Tibet, he says, while others arriving from the Chinese side were also in the area."Those who completed the immigration formalities that morning, I don't think were able to complete their immigration process on the Chinese side," Pokharel tells the BBC.Pokharel says it took 15 to 20 minutes to walk from the Nepalese immigration office to the bridge after travellers had cleared immigration. Travellers arriving late the previous afternoon sometimes had to wait until the border reopened the next morning, while those travelling in groups or by bus would often wait for everyone to clear immigration before moving on together.That makes it difficult to know where those 89 people were when the flood struck.At 08:37 - less than two minutes after the immigration system recorded its final transaction - seismic instruments detected movement in the mountains above the border, according to a timeline compiled by Nepal's Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research. Researchers later attributed the signal to the collapse of part of a glacier that triggered the flood.China said the mudslide reached the border crossing from its origin in around seven minutes.People at the crossing could have been making their way towards the bridge, waiting in Ghatte Khola or preparing to cross towards the Chinese facility. Exactly where each person was remains unclear.And Ghatte Khola itself was far more than a waiting area. Pokharel says 50 to 60 houses stood there, alongside hotels, local businesses and four hydropower offices.It was also the final stop for buses from Kathmandu, and a base for drivers, helpers, tourist guides and cargo workers waiting for customs clearance. Travellers heading into Tibet often queued there from the previous day."My 40-50 close friends are missing," Pokharel said. Pokharel believes the toll there could be far higher than official figures suggest, estimating that "2,000 to 2,500 people" may have been caught in the flood. The figure is his estimate and has not been independently verified.The immigration office itself stood about 100 metres above the river, Pokharel says. But during the flood, the water appeared to surge even higher. He initially hoped his missing colleagues might have escaped to grazing land several kilometres away.For some of the Indian pilgrims at the border, the morning had begun almost casually. They made video calls and reels for relatives back home, showing them the mountains as they waited for the Chinese immigration office to open.Sudipto Bhattacharya was receiving messages from his wife, Subhrasree Chakraborty, who was travelling with a group of more than 60 people. At 07:57 Nepal time, she sent him a photograph of the departure stamp in her passport: Nepalese immigration was done. Six minutes later, at 08:03, she sent another message: "We are waiting to enter China." Then the messages stopped.Among those at the Chinese immigration facility was a group of 77 pilgrims associated with the Isha Foundation, returning from Mount Kailash. They, along with three staff members, were unaccounted for after the flood swept through the area.When a 21-member Chinese rescue team reached Gyirong on 28 August, one rescuer told Chinese state media: "As far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins."The crossing had only recently recovered from another major flood. In July 2025, flooding shut Rasuwagadhi for nearly six months. It reopened on 1 January after China built a temporary bridge.Traffic had since returned. Chinese border authorities say more than 100,000 people had passed through Gyirong by June, while Nepali immigration records show 53,742 arrivals and departures at Rasuwagadhi in the year to mid-July. The two figures are based on different reporting periods and counting systems, making a direct comparison difficult.Indians were the largest group recorded at the Nepali immigration point, followed by Nepalis and Chinese.Gyirong had also become one of the main arteries linking Nepal and China.Posh Raj Pandey, chairman emeritus of the Kathmandu-based South Asia Watch on Trade, Economics and Environment, says Rasuwagadhi is one of Nepal's two main trading points with China, alongside Tatopani, and accounts for about a third of Nepal's $2.95bn trade with its northern neighbour.Around 60 to 70 trucks passed through the gorge each day, carrying electronics, machinery, vehicles, fruit, clothing and other goods towards Kathmandu. Pandey says the route also handled about 80% of Nepal's electric-vehicle imports from China.Its closure has left Nepal increasingly dependent on Tatopani - which Chinese authorities have also temporarily closed, external because of landslide risks on the Nepali side, the Kathmandu Post reports. The crossing also lies along the proposed route of the railway connecting the region to Kathmandu, part of plans by Nepal and China to develop a trans-Himalayan rail network."Nepal should develop an alternative China trade route and reconsider its wider development strategy, including its heavy concentration of hydropower projects along the same river system," Pandey says. "We have put all eggs here. We need to develop an alternative border port."Across the border, Pokharel was left thinking about conversations he had with the colleagues who were now missing.The previous year's flood had made staff at the Rasuwagadhi immigration office acutely aware of the danger. At night, he says, they sometimes "felt vibrations" and went outside to check the river. They had even discussed among themselves about escaping uphill if another flood struck."But my friends could not get that chance," he said.

articles.title: Children sleeping on piles of clothes, says charity
articles.summary: A Peterborough charity says hundreds of children in the city are living in bed poverty.
articles.body: Children sleeping on piles of clothes, says charityImage caption, Ashley Wilcox from Care Zone said families came to them asking for help with basic furniture itemsByKate Moser AndonBBC political reporter, CambridgeshireA furniture bank said it has been helping families whose children were sleeping on floors, piles of clothes and other makeshift beds.Peterborough-based Care Zone, which has a warehouse on the edge of the city, plans to spend £80,000 this year on beds and mattresses for local families."Many children are sleeping on a pile of clothes, or maybe just on the hard floor," said Ashley Wilcox from Care Zone, adding: "That's not good enough."Peterborough City Council said it was working with local charities to reach as many families in crisis as possible.Image caption, The warehouse stores everything from beds and sofas to long-life food itemsCare Zone is one of several organisations part of the council's crisis resilience fund, a network helping people with food parcels, advice and other services.Its volunteers clean and repair donated furniture and other household goods, giving out more than 3,500 larger items last year and 425 smaller items, such as saucepans and tin openers.Of the 1,900 people who used Care Zone last year, about 845 were children.This year the warehouse is piled high with brand new mattresses ready for families in need."We see families that have basically been in temporary accommodation," said Wilcox."There might be a family of five in one single room sharing a few beds, sleeping on the floor, nowhere to cook."He said tackling bed poverty was a priority because of the impact it had on children's education."For children in particular, a good night's sleep is really essential."By giving them a bed, they have a much better chance at doing better in school."Anyone can donate items to Care Zone, and it is accessed by people being referred through organisations such as the council or their GP.Image caption, Esther Baffa-Isaacs said the council was writing directly to households facing financial crisisEsther Baffa-Isaacs, from the city council's poverty prevention team, said there was "much more we can do" to reach people in crisis.She said the authority recently wrote letters to 3,200 households in the city which it had identified as being in a "crisis state", to check they were claiming the correct benefits and knew where to find support."That was what it came down to, just saying, 'you have help'," she said.A recent study by Policy in Practice found people in Peterborough were missing out on £92m from unclaimed benefits.Baffa-Isaacs said bed poverty was a "significant" issue where the authority was "very keen to do more".She said: "Child bed poverty is significant, and it has an impact on educational attainment."Image caption, Zameer Ali urged people in Peterborough to ask for help if they need itAbout one-third of children in Peterborough are thought to be living in poverty, according to data, external from 2024 and 2025 published by the Department for Work and Pensions, compared with a UK average of 26%.Zameer Ali, Peterborough City Council's cabinet member for communities and public safety and a Labour councillor, said the authority was "doing everything" to reach people.He said language barriers could be a problem, and wanted information to be as easy as possible to understand, for example where a parent may be asking their child to translate for them."We don't want you to go without and we certainly do not want you or your children to fall into any form of hardship," he said."What you need to do is reach back to us and say 'I need help'."Do you have a story suggestion for Peterborough? Contact us below.Get in touchMore from PeterboroughRelated internet links

articles.title: Hospitality wants permanent VAT cut, 'not gimmick'
articles.summary: Hospitality sector members call for a temporary VAT reduction scheme to be widened and extended.
articles.body: Since the end of June until 1 September, VAT was reduced on children's meals served in restaurants, as well as kids' and family tickets for cinemas, shows, exhibitions and outdoor venues and activities.Tara Stapley, the general manager of the Big Sheep Farm and Theme Park in  Bideford in north Devon, said: "Numbers have increased slightly and I think that is partly down to the summer savings scheme."The business reduced ticket prices and added more children's meals to the menu.Stapley said there were "lots of people calling and asking about it".She said: "People coming have been quite pleasantly surprised by our ticket prices and we're saying we're part of the summer savings scheme and they have been very grateful for that."Stapley added the scheme could have been publicised more as "a lot of people didn't know about it".She backed any extension of the scheme "100%, if that happened we'd be dancing on the ceiling I think" and said it would be helpful for families and businesses over the October half term and Halloween.Stapley said days out can be expensive: "We want to make that as affordable as possible and memories that last a lifetime for them."Anything that the government can do in extending the scheme would be a huge help not only for us but the people who want to visit our site as well."Southwell, also chair of the Cornwall Association of Tourist Attractions, said he had initially thought it was "a great idea".He added: "But I know some attractions have not reduced the price but taken that money and used it for their attraction, which, in fairness, is fine because otherwise they might have had to have put their prices up."He said a permanent 0% or 5% VAT rate for attractions "would allow all of us to invest for the future".Lappa Valley head of marketing Matt Bunt said it was "amazing that families are able to keep a bit more money in their pockets", but added the "policy was put out in a bit of a rush and not very well publicised by the government".Visit Devon's director Sally Everton said the scheme should have run to 1 November, to cover the autumn half term and the pre-schoolers whose families go on holiday after the main summer break, rather than finishing at the end of the August bank holiday weekend.Some venues in Devon offered "kids eat fee on some meals "as it was easier to manage and was a "real buy-in point for a lot of people".Everton said some venues told her "it's not worth it" as they found it a "logistical nightmare".She said the move was welcome but thought cuts should be "broader and it needs to be permanent"."The VAT is a killer to so many businesses."  "In an ideal world a reduced VAT across a broader hospitality sector and permanently would be the ideal situation."A Treasury spokesperson said: "Our Great British Summer Savings has benefitted businesses and families from across the South West. "The scheme is increasing footfall for businesses over the summer, getting more people through the door and boosting local economies."This is on top of the chancellor cutting business rates by 20% for pubs, social clubs and live music venues - saving thousands of locals over £1,000 a year."Follow BBC Cornwall on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to spotlight@bbc.co.uk, external.

articles.title: We survived the Aberfan disaster as schoolchildren, but were told to never talk about it again
articles.summary: In one of Britain's worst disasters, 116 children were killed on the morning of 21 October 1966.
articles.body: Image caption, Janett was the only child on her street to return home from school on the day of the disasterByHuw ThomasBBC Wales correspondentReporting fromAberfan and Tony BrownBBC WalesUpdated 1 September 2026 06:12 BSTJanett Bickley almost stayed home from school on the morning of 21 October 1966.The eight-year-old had recently recovered from pneumonia, but she was determined to go in for the last day before half-term.Shortly after taking her seat at Pantglas Junior School, Janett was buried beneath tonnes of coal slurry from a collapsing tip. It engulfed the classrooms and killed 144 people, including 116 children.Sixty years later, Janett is one of the many survivors of the Aberfan disaster whose lives were shaped by what they experienced."I've always wanted to do something to pay back to the community because I think I owed something to the community, because I lived," she said.The sentiment is echoed by other Aberfan survivors, who went on to devote much of their lives to helping others through education, public service, community work and charity.Image source, Janett BickleyImage caption, Janett (front row, second left) with her nursery classmates in 1964. Many of the children in this photograph died in the disaster, two years laterJanett has a clear memory of the aftermath of the disaster.A classmate dug her out from the wreckage. She recalls climbing through broken rafters before joining a queue of children waiting to be pulled through a window to safety. Later, she discovered that she had been the only child from her street to return home from school that day.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, When a colliery waste tip collapsed, slurry crashed into Pantglas Junior School, killing 116 children and 28 adultsDespite the shared trauma, survivors rarely discussed what had happened."We were lucky, 'You lived, don't speak about it ever again'," Janett recalled being told.The message was repeated across many households."It wasn't discussed at all," she added. "We were way into our 30s or 40s before we even talked about it for the first time together."Image source, Janett BickleyImage caption, Janett in December 1967, a little over a year after the disasterFor Denise Morgan, the silence came after tragedy struck her own family.She had recently started grammar school after passing the 11-plus examination when her younger sister, Annette, was killed in the disaster. The shock and grief changed everything."When I came to take my O-levels as they were then, I failed them all miserably apart from one," she said. "The family were traumatised. My parents were traumatised."Image source, Family PhotoImage caption, Denise and her younger sister Annette, who was killed in the disasterFor decades, many survivors kept their memories private. Janett said children had often been encouraged to look forward rather than back."We all went to a psychiatrist, and we never spoke about it, even to the psychiatrist," said Denise.It was not until she was an adult, when former classmates began sharing their experiences, that some found relief."When we finally broke that seal of talking about it, it healed us, in a way," she said. Denise said many survivors had gone on to lead successful lives, while others had continued to struggle."You can see it in some people in Aberfan. They have come through it. Others have not, and suffered for many years."Image caption, Denise became a head teacher and was appointed an MBE for services to educationFor Denise, helping others began with a promise she made long before the disaster.As a pupil at Pantglas, she had been inspired by her teachers and decided she wanted to follow in their footsteps."I knew at 11 that I wanted to be a teacher," she said.But the path was far from straightforward.Grief affected her education, but she remained determined, and eventually she qualified, became a head teacher, and later received an MBE for services to education. Much of her career was spent supporting children from disadvantaged backgrounds and encouraging them to believe in their own potential."I often told my story," she said, sharing with schoolchildren: "You can be anything you want to be."Looking back today, she still thinks about the teachers she lost."They all helped to save many of the children that are alive today."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Jeff Edwards was one of the last children to be pulled alive from Pantglas Junior School"They always contact us in Aberfan after the damage to see how we survived, how we coped," he said. "It's good to help others get through major disasters and traumas."Jeff believes his own response to Aberfan emerged years after the disaster.After establishing a career in accountancy and working in London, he returned home in the mid-1990s to find many local young people struggling in the aftermath of pit closures and industrial decline.Image caption, Jeff returned to Aberfan and feared a second generation of young people would be lost "I think the reason I really came back was those youngsters hanging about the street with no future. It was the second generation who were being lost to the community," he said.Many had left school without qualifications. Some were involved in crime, drugs and alcohol, and two local young people had taken their own lives.Using grants from organisations including Children in Need, Jeff helped to create projects focused on literacy, support for parents, employment and youth engagement. Some went on to transform lives, helping people into jobs and university.Jeff became adept at accessing grants and even had a donation from the late queen for one of his projects to help young people, though he cannot reveal the amount she sent."I've begged, stolen and borrowed to ensure that we've got the right resources for the young people of the village," he said.Later, as an independent councillor and then leader of the council, he helped secure funding for projects across Merthyr Tydfil and championed investment in education and community development.Looking back, he believes helping others also helped him."By helping them, I was helping myself, in terms of my own recovery process," he said.Image source, I.C. Rapoport/Getty ImagesImage caption, David Davies was pictured on the family farm near Pantglas Junior School in the weeks after the Aberfan disasterDavid Davies was sitting at his desk in Pantglas School when the tip collapsed. The debris knocked him unconscious."I was brought out and was initially placed with the deceased bodies and covered with a blanket in the playground area, until someone thought they saw my foot move," David recalled."I was evidently still alive and taken off to hospital where I was in intensive care for a little while. But actually I managed to get out of hospital in time for Bonfire night."David was the subject of photos by the renowned photographer Chuck Rapoport, who visited Aberfan in the days after the disaster.After recovering from serious head injuries, David attended a school outside the village and believed that separation from former classmates may have sheltered him from some of the trauma experienced by others."I did not witness anything that might have been going on around the school because I was unconscious. So I never had any ongoing issues with PTSD or anything like that, and thankfully I'd never had any long-term issues with my head injuries either," he said.David studied at Aberystwyth and Cambridge before building a successful career in international law.But after returning home, he increasingly devoted his time to public service.He became a magistrate, served with housing organisations and has spent 26 years as chair of the Aberfan memorial charity, which is responsible for preserving Aberfan's memorial sites.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, David took the Prince and Princess of Wales around the Aberfan memorial garden in 2023What motivates David remains clear."I'm clearly grateful to have survived an experience that half of my classmates did not," he said."It's really in their honour and in their memory that I'm driven forward, and have been over the last 26 years, to achieve fitting memorial sites both here at the memorial garden and the cemetery and other memorials to victims, so that they will be of a standard that will be fitting of their memory and acceptable to the community both here in Wales and further afield."He added: "I think the Queen put it in the words of 'an indomitable spirit' in the community. And I think that really sums it up in terms of what this community has gone through, how it's recovered, and the difference it's made to the community as a whole."Image caption, Janett recently got a tattoo of a clock that shows the time of the disasterFor Janett, the urge to give something back intensified during the Covid-19 pandemic.After a 30-year career in the pharmaceutical industry, she found herself looking out of her window and thinking about the isolation and loneliness affecting the community around her.Her campaign to install a Christmas tree in Aberfan soon grew into something much bigger.Working with volunteers, she helped secure funding for Christmas lights, community celebrations, carnival events and local projects designed to bring people together."The wellbeing of the community was ripped apart and it took a long time to build back up," she said.Today she also campaigns for the future of community facilities, supports local scouting and is working to ensure a community events organisation can continue after she steps back."All of a sudden the community is getting together, and I love it," she said.The disaster itself remains with her.Recently she had an image of a clock, frozen at 09:13 on 21 October 1966, tattooed on her arm."It is with me for life," said Janett.'We're lucky - we lived'Survivors and families who were affected by the Aberfan disaster have all done very different things with their lives, but many have found ways to honour those children who never had the chance to grow up.For Janett, it comes back to a simple belief."We feel lucky," she said."We're lucky we lived. Let's make this work. Let's do something for the community, because we're obviously here for a reason."If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.More top stories

articles.title: Djokovic's tearful loss leaves future uncertain
articles.summary: After Novak Djokovic's latest bid for a historic 25th major title ends in tears in New York, where does the most decorated men's player of the Open era go from here?
articles.body: Be warned: Novak Djokovic has made a fool of those who have doubted him before.Some questioned if the Serb would challenge for the sport's top honours again after he dropped out of the world's top 20 amid a two-year major title drought in 2018.Djokovic proceeded to win four of the following five Grand Slams, doubling his tally of majors with 12 across the next six years.But three years have now passed since he landed his men's record 24th major title at the US Open.And, as the 39-year-old fought back tears mid-match on Sunday night, this latest loss in New York felt different.Staring at a first opening-round Grand Slam exit since 2006, one of sport's all-time greats simply had nothing left, beaten 7-6 (7-5) 5-7 4-6 6-2 6-1 by Argentina's Navone.For so long now Djokovic has not only defied time, but appeared to be improving with it.That was evident at this year's Wimbledon, where he outlasted Felix Auger-Aliassime, 14 years his junior, in a five-set thriller that became the longest quarter-final in the tournament's history.Even in his late 30s, Djokovic has been the one challenging Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz, the new dominant forces in the men's game.At the Australian Open in January, he ended Sinner's bid for a third-straight title in a sensational five-set comeback victory. He then led Alcaraz by a set in the final, before fading to a four-set defeat.After early exits in Paris and New York, there is an inevitable sense that Melbourne was his best chance to secure an outright record 25th major triumph and cap a career unparalleled in every statistical measure.Djokovic was despondent after the match, saying he "despised every moment I spent on the court for that"."When it comes to the match itself, and the overall feeling of how I felt with my body and playing, it was really not enjoyable," Djokovic said."But, from the perspective of the crowd and support, it was incredible."I'm very sorry that I didn't perform as well as I should have, could have, or wanted - for them."The four-time winner's shock first-round US Open defeat means:Djokovic will drop out of the world's top 10 for the first time since July 2018His record streak of 78 successive wins in first-round matches at Grand Slams is overAs is his perfect 37-0 record in the first two rounds at the US OpenHe suffered a first-round exit at a major for the first time in 20 years, when the then 76th-ranked Serb lost at the 2006 Australian OpenDjokovic's refusal to disappear from contention on the sport's biggest stages has prolonged the final embers of the 'Big Three' era that captivated crowds for the best part of two decades.But, for the first time in almost 24 years, the next world ranking update will have a top 10 missing at least one of Djokovic, Rafael Nadal or Roger Federer.Nadal, a 22-time major winner, called time on his career aged 38 in 2024, two years after 20-time slam champion Roger Federer did so aged 41.While Djokovic, who will turn 40 next May, is still going, they all share one thing in common - they each last won a slam aged 36.Ken Rosewall remains the oldest men's singles slam champion in the Open era, winning the 1972 Australian Open two months after turning 37.There is no doubt that the game has become far more physically demanding over the 54 years since.Djokovic prevented Federer from breaking Rosewall's record when he saved two championship points to win the 2019 Wimbledon final, one month before the Swiss turned 38.And early exits are still rare for Djokovic at the Grand Slams. He has reached at least the semi-finals eight times at the past 12 majors.Since winning his last slam, Djokovic achieved his lifelong goal of winning Olympic gold at Paris 2024.With that triumph - two months after knee surgery and three weeks after losing to the Spaniard in the Wimbledon final - Djokovic became only the fifth player to complete the career 'Golden Slam'.Since then, his attention has been on breaking his tie with Margaret Court of 24 major singles titles.He has slimmed down his schedule to prioritise the majors. In 2026 he has contested just seven tournaments - four Grand Slams and three Masters 1000 events - and his 21 Tour-level matches are his fewest in a season since 2004.Reacting to Djokovic's defeat, former Wimbledon champion Pat Cash said on BBC Radio 5 Live: "You can't substitute matchplay. You can't be walking into a Grand Slam on a hot and humid day and expect to get through a five-set match. "I know he's super-human in many ways but it's going to catch up with you."Djokovic has stated his desire to continue in the sport until the next Olympics, in Los Angeles in 2028.It would be a fitting stage for his farewell - not least that it would be exactly a decade since his ability to still compete for the biggest prizes was first questioned.Discussing retirement in his recently released documentary, Djokovic said: 'Why would I talk about retirement when I still keep proving to myself that I can still win?'But, as of Sunday night, legitimate doubt has been cast on whether that remains true.

articles.title: B&B boss fears 'uneven playing field' over tourist tax
articles.summary: The introduction of a tourism levy in North Yorkshire is currently under consideration.
articles.body: Image source, BBC/RICHARD EDWARDSImage caption, James (left) and Angela Rusden at Scarborough's Toulson Court B&BByRichard EdwardsNorth Yorkshire political reporterA Scarborough bed and breakfast owner has said businesses like his will face an "uneven playing field" if a so-called tourist tax is introduced in North Yorkshire but not in neighbouring East Yorkshire.A consultation on plans for a visitor levy closed in February and legislation is expected to be brought forward later this year.James Rusden, who runs Scarborough's Toulson Court B&B, said if the levy was not England-wide, cost-of-living pressures would mean some visitors would instead go where no tourist tax was being charged.A government spokesperson said: "We're listening to businesses in Yorkshire and across the country on this so we make sure money raised is invested in local priorities."Rusden said he believed such a levy would act like "a form of taxation"."Nobody likes an extra cost and people will complain about it," he said."But if it was an even playing field it would be a lot better as it would be easier to manage and control."People are short of money. To put a tax on them coming on holiday makes them think twice about where they go."If someone is coming to Scarborough but has to pay a levy each night, but can go to Bridlington where there's no levy, then that's where they'll go. "It's unfair and it'll make it harder for us to compete."Image source, BBC/PRITTI MISTRYImage caption, Businesses in Scarborough's North Bay could be some of those affected by a visitor levyRusden said he was also concerned about the time the levy could be introduced, as people continued to struggle with the cost of living and faced further increases to energy bills.A record season at Scarborough's Open Air Theatre, with its string of sold-out shows, had kept some North Bay B&Bs in business this year, Rusden said."We have a fantastic reputation and have won some good awards," he said."But we've discussed whether one of us has to go out and get a job to make up the difference and run the business differently."People used to come for four or five nights, they're now knocking a night off. They just can't afford it."'Drawbacks and opportunities'York and North Yorkshire's elected Labour mayor David Skaith said he believed a visitor levy "could be a total game-changer for us"."York and North Yorkshire is beautiful, with something for everyone. Millions of people visit every year," he explained."Our visitor levy report was commissioned to understand the drawbacks and opportunities of the levy. We are taking time to review the feedback before we take our next steps."However, Luke Campbell, Reform UK mayor for Hull and East Yorkshire, has previously said a levy would "not be the right approach" for his region. Prof Brendan Paddison, Dean of York St John University's business school and chair of York Tourism Advisory Board, said research at the university has found a need to keep the tourism industry engaged in "decision-making and governance processes" around any proposed visitor levy."It also found a need that some of that funding that is perhaps raised through a levy is ring-fenced to support the industry and the work it does," Paddison said.Image source, BBC/RICHARD EDWARDSImage caption, Scarborough holidaymakers Charlie Highnett (left) and Phil and Carol Smith with Logan the dog (right)In Scarborough's North Bay, Phil and Carol Smith said they would still visit the resort even if a tourism levy was introduced.Visiting from Derbyshire along with Logan the border terrier, Phil said he and Carol were married in Scarborough, stayed there at least three times a year and called the town their "second home".Phil said he did not think a levy of £1 to £2 a night on an overnight stay would stop them making the trip."I'd rather not pay it, but that's nothing. A pint of Guinness is almost six quid, what's a pound? We feel comfortable here, everyone's so friendly."However, both Phil and Carol questioned how and where the money would be invested, saying, for instance, that Scarborough needed more public toilets."It's a busy town. Some more places to sit, and especially some more public toilets, would be money well spent," Carol said.'Joint decisions'Meanwhile, Charlie Highnett, who lives in East Yorkshire, said he would shop around accommodation providers for a cheaper deal in North Yorkshire in a bid to offset the cost of any levy."We really like coming to Scarborough, but it would be disappointing to pay any extra," he said."People want to come here and enjoy their holidays. I don't think any additional tax is needed, but if it is introduced it should be unified - not just one county."He added that there should be "some alignment and joint decisions made".Rod Fretwell, visiting Scarborough from his home in Bolton, said if the levy was being implemented nationally, he would support it."But if it singles out some businesses, like hotels and bed and breakfasts, and doesn't cover others, and it's not national - so you can go down the road and they don't charge it - then it shouldn't be done," he said.Image source, BBC/RICHARD EDWARDSImage caption, Rod Fretwell - visiting Scarborough from Bolton - said the visitor levy should be implemented nationallyPaddison said the findings of the consultation in North Yorkshire would provide "key industry insights" into the implications of any levy being introduced."There will also be learning from other countries and other areas in Europe that have a levy and the impact it's had - not just in terms of visitor numbers and the revenue generated, but how that money's spent," he said.Skaith said: "We must get this right, because if we do, we can invest in what makes our county a fantastic place to live and visit like never before."The government spokesperson said ministers were "delivering the biggest transfer of power, funding and responsibility from Westminster in a generation".Mayors' new powers to introduce such a levy would mean local people benefited "even more" from tourism to their area, they said."When places grow their economies, they keep more of the rewards and can invest in what matters most to their communities."Figure caption, Would tourist tax deter a North Yorkshire holiday?Get in touchMore on this story

articles.title: 'Rare' council underspend to help with cost of living
articles.summary: It will not, however, be used to offset any potential future increase to council tax."At this time, we think it's better value for the taxpayer to take that £20m underspend and invest it into the services that they want to see improvement in," Radford said.The council effectively declared itself bankrupt in 2023 but has recently shown signs of recovery.Commissioners appointed t…
articles.body: It will not, however, be used to offset any potential future increase to council tax."At this time, we think it's better value for the taxpayer to take that £20m underspend and invest it into the services that they want to see improvement in," Radford said.The council effectively declared itself bankrupt in 2023 but has recently shown signs of recovery.Commissioners appointed to help run the authority in 2024 left earlier this year and were replaced with "ministerial envoys", who have fewer powers.Radford said an underspend was "quite rare" but was evidence of the council's improving financial position.Kirsty L Jones, leader of the Nottingham People's Alliance, however, said it may have come as a result of "under-delivery of services in the first place"."I think when they've cut so deeply previously, it's not going to cause any sort of recovery in the services people expect, paying higher council tax for fewer services as they've seen throughout the years," she said."Helping with the cost of living - I don't know how they can meaningfully do that with £20m and expect to spend it on other things too."The use of the underspend funds will be discussed at a meeting of the council's executive board on Tuesday.It will then require approval from full council because it constitutes a change to the authority's annual budget.

articles.title: Why the issue of early prisoner release is playing out differently in Scotland
articles.summary: Letting prisoners out early to ease prison overcrowding is proving politically fraught both sides of the border.
articles.body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Glasgow's Barlinnie prison has been described as severely overcrowdedByDavid CowanScotland home affairs correspondent and Andrew PickenBBC Scotland data visualisation unitThe fury over the potential early release in England of the two teenagers who killed PC Andrew Harper has focused public attention on prison overcrowding in a way that hasn't happened in Scotland.The Scottish government has ventured into similarly contentious territory as it tries to find a long-term solution to Scotland's record-breaking prison population.But the absence of such a controversial case has largely kept the story out of the headlines.The key proposal from the SNP administration is to bring forward the automatic release point for hundreds of people convicted of offences including rape and culpable homicide - Scotland's version of manslaughter.Even if those plans are implemented, many Scottish criminals will still have to serve a greater proportion of their sentence behind bars than those convicted of the same offence in England and Wales.That doesn't necessarily mean Scotland is tougher on crime than England and Wales. Down south, prison sentences for the most serious crimes are often longer.This issue is playing out differently on both sides of the border. What is happening with prisoner early release in England?Since 2024, tens of thousands of inmates have been let out early to create more space in England's prisons.From the start of next month, the Sentencing Act passed by Sir Keir Starmer's government will see some prisoners let out after serving a third of their sentence.Those who would previously have served two-thirds will instead be released after serving half of their term.Multiple exemptions have been applied in recent months in response to a backlash from the public and opposition politicians.These started with the announcement that sentences for rape and child sex offences would not be covered by the change.In response to the furore over PC Harper's case, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said anyone convicted of unlawful killing - including all forms of manslaughter - will be excluded from the scheme.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, There has been widespread public outrage at the proposal to release PC Andrew Harper's killersHow many prisoners have been given emergency early release in Scotland so far?Almost 1,100 short-term prisoners - those serving less than four years - have been freed early to ease the pressure on the system, a policy backed by the Scottish Parliament.In the summer of 2024, a total of 477 were granted emergency early release. Prisoners convicted of sex offences or domestic abuse were excluded and governors could veto the release of certain prisoners if they had concerns about public safety.By December that year, 61 had been returned to custody - approximately 13% of the total released.A second wave between November 2025 and April this year saw the emergency early release of 614 inmates, again with the same exemptions. Full figures aren't yet available but at least 34 have been returned to custody.What other changes have been implemented in Scotland?With Holyrood's support, the rules on the automatic release point for short-term prisoners have been changed twice, introducing exemptions for people convicted of sex offences and domestic abuse. Early last year, the release point was brought forward from 50% of the sentence to 40%, resulting in the immediate release of 312 prisoners. A further reduction from 40% to 30% saw 240 prisoners freed immediately between May and July this year.What other proposals have been put forward in Scotland?Under the current scheme in Scotland, long-term prisoners - those serving four years or more - become eligible for parole halfway through their prison sentence.  If they don't get parole, they are freed automatically when they have six months left to serve.The Scottish government wants to change the automatic release point to two-thirds of the sentence.This would apply to all long-term prisoners, including people convicted of unlawful killing, rape, child abuse, drug trafficking, and attempted murder.The proposals are complex, but if they were backed by parliament at least 630 prisoners would be freed straight away.Another proposal would change the designation for short-term prisoners to those serving under five years.Groups representing victims of crime have called for exemptions for sex offenders and people convicted of domestic abuse.Excluding those offenders would reduce the impact of the proposed change.Ministers will have to decide whether to press ahead regardless of the controversy, or scale down what they hope to achieve.First Minister John Swinney has said some valid points have been made about exemptions, which could signal a possible change of heart from him.Andy Burham wants to end IPP sentences - does Scotland have them?English and Welsh courts imposed Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences between 2005 and 2012, on offenders deemed to pose a significant risk of causing serious harm to the public.Once the minimum jail term which was fixed by the judge had been served, the prisoner could only be released if the parole board decided it was safe to do so.The government stopped giving new IPP sentences because they caused extreme delays in release.But many prisoners are still serving them. According to the Ministry of Justice, 2,271 people were serving IPP sentences in June. Of those, 856 have never been released.Burnham plans to table legislation to terminate IPPs during the current parliament. That would end what is a controversial policy, and free up space in jails in England and Wales.In Scotland, judges can impose an Order for Lifelong Restriction (OLR), which combines a minimum prison term, release sanctioned by the parole board, and lifelong monitoring in the community.More than 270 have been imposed since 1999, and a far smaller proportion of prisoners on OLRs have been released compared to IPPs.Campaigners have claimed that the sentences could amount to inhumane and degrading treatment. .So far, the Scottish government has shown no signs of wanting to end OLRs.Why is prison overcrowding a serious issue - and what's coming next?In Scotland, more than 8,500 prisoners are being held in a system designed for 7,805, placing prison staff and inmates under pressure and reducing time that can be spent on rehabilitation.An increase in the number and length of long-term sentences is contributing to the problem.A huge rise in the number of cases being sent to the high court for prosecution is likely to boost the prison population even further.Two new jails are under construction. The government and prison service are looking at increasing capacity with the use of modular accommodation. An average prison place costs over £50,000 a year.SNP administrations have been in charge of Scotland's justice system since 2007 and say tackling overcrowding is "of critical importance".Ministers want the courts to reduce the number of jail terms under two years and make greater use of "robust" community-based sentences.A consultation process has been completed. The government is now drawing up its proposals to present to parliament.More on this story

articles.title: 'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban
articles.summary: As of August, the number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran had reached another million.
articles.body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC's Lyse Doucet reports on the biggest cross-border movement of peopleByLyse DoucetChief international correspondentReporting fromTorkham crossing and KabulThe elderly grimace, hobbling on crutches, and wide-eyed children stare, cradling chickens carried from homes they were forced to leave behind."It feels good to be in my own country," 35-year-old Nazia says, just minutes after she crosses from Pakistan, where she was born, into Afghanistan.The Torkham crossing, known as "Zero Point", is where one hard life ends and another begins."But I've never been to Afghanistan before and many people here don't even have enough bread to eat," Nazia sighs as she heads, two of her children in tow, toward registration counters festooned with white and black Taliban flags.Nearly her entire family, eight sisters and their offspring, were deported to Afghanistan this year from Pakistan or Iran.They are part of the biggest cross-border movement of people anywhere in the world.Millions of Afghans have fled across the borders to Pakistan and Iran for decades – seeking refuge or employment - and the number escaping Afghanistan has continued to rise since the Taliban takeover in August 2021.Most are now being forced to return as these two neighbours crack down on undocumented migrants. Nazia and her family were undocumented but the UN and human rights groups say the security sweep is reaching far beyond that group to include registered Afghans too. Even Pakistan now publicly says that Afghans with Proof of Registration cards are not exempt.The expulsions show no sign of stopping. Image source, AFPImage caption, Trucks carrying returnees parked along the highway near the border The number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran has already reached another million, according to the UN's Refugee Agency, the UNHCR."In a little under three years, we've seen six million people, a population that is itself the size of a small country, come back to Afghanistan," observes Charlie Goodlake, spokesperson for the UNHCR in Afghanistan."We've never seen in recent history a return movement on this scale," he underlines, standing in the baking heat in the tented village close to the border.It's a desolate landscape of tarpaulin and plastic shelters, many now tattered and torn, erected by the UN and other aid agencies to provide refuge for a few nights for a people arriving with nowhere to go.Many returnees have not set foot in Afghanistan for decades; many like Nazia have never been here at all."I left 45 years ago during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and most of my brothers were born in Pakistan," explains Sarwar, who arrived a few days earlier with seven brothers and their families in a convoy of 40 people and the jumble of their worldly goods packed into a lumbering Pakistani lorry."We spent a long time there, so of course I felt heartbroken when they forced us out of our home," he says. "But, despite all that pain, I am also happy because I am finally free of harassment by Pakistan's police."Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Afghan returnees deported from Pakistan arriving at the Torkham crossing Every family we met told us they had experienced prejudice and harassment by authorities in Pakistan.The Pakistan government has not responded to the BBC's questions, but a foreign ministry spokesman told a briefing in Islamabad on Sunday that "the Government of Pakistan undertakes the necessary measures to prevent any instance of harassment or maltreatment of Afghan nationals in Pakistan. If such incidents have taken place, they are sporadic and are dealt with fully in accordance with the law". Both Pakistan and Iran say it's past time for Afghans to go home, accusing some of posing a security risk, and others of being a financial burden.The expulsions from Pakistan and alleged abuse intensified after a major escalation in fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan last October. In February, Human Rights Watch highlighted "door-to-door raids, late-night home searches and arrests without warrants".In Iran, which claimed last year to host more than four million undocumented Afghans, the mass deportations were accelerated after its 12-day war with Israel and the US in June 2025.The New York based Centre for Human Rights in Iran accused the authorities of using the post-war climate to "cast suspicion on Afghan migrants - accusing them of espionage and branding them as potential spies for Israel".The UN's refugee agency continues to underscore the humanitarian principle that any return should be "voluntary, safe and dignified".But in Torkham, Sarwar's sister-in-law Zarina laments the precarious future they face: "We have no resources to start a business or earn a living, and we don't even own a tent to live in".Image caption, Zarina, 40, is among the million Afghan who have returned this year alone Inside the barren transit tent, which provides little escape from scorching 41C heat, Zarina sits alongside an anxious huddle of women and their children. Are they worried about the future for women and girls in a country where the Taliban has barred women from much of public life, including secondary school and university?Forty-year-old Zarina turns to make a sweeping gesture with her arm: "Look at them, they're all girls. Of course I'm worried."Some returnees are not just worried; they're terrified."I don't leave this house," a former Afghan security guard, first deported from Iran and then Pakistan, nervously tells us when we meet him far from the border in what he hopes is a safe house. "We are all living in fear including my wife and children who are also afraid to go outside."He dismisses the Taliban government's amnesty, announced days after their return to power which declared that former government officials, security personnel and civil servants would not face retaliation and were encouraged to return to work."I have no trust in their amnesty because many of my colleagues have been killed." He says his case had been registered with the UN but was deported before he could be transferred to a safer country. Financial hardship magnifies the pain. The steep cuts in foreign aid worldwide are especially sharp in Afghanistan where the Taliban are still stuck in sanctions linked to terrorism and human rights.Pakistan confirmed on Sunday that 16,000 vulnerable Afghans have now been granted, on humanitarian grounds, a temporary exemption from being deported – a decision welcomed by the UN.  But sources estimate that the number of Afghans in Pakistan at risk of serious harm, including women and girls who would be denied education, could be as high as 250,000.Image caption, Zarina says she is worried about the future of the girls who cannot attend secondary school and university in Taliban-run AfghanistanAt the graceful foreign ministry compound in Kabul, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi tries to put on a brave face."There's no doubt that we need some help," he admits. "There is pressure due to their return but in the long run, it will benefit them as well as Afghanistan."In the first years after the Taliban swept to power in 2021, some of their ministers made light of humanitarian issues, saying God would provide. The UN now estimates that 21.9 million people, nearly half the country, need assistance this year to survive. The UN's children agency, UNICEF, said last week that one million children faced "life-threatening" malnutrition."No country in the world could handle this kind of crisis on its own," UNHCR spokesperson Goodlake assesses, while acknowledging Taliban government efforts to help returnees as they arrive.But, he adds, "We also know that many of the restrictions and edicts they put in place, particularly on women and girls, don't help us elicit international support".Muttaqi reiterates his government's line that matters like girl's education are "internal issues" for Afghans to resolve.The severe restrictions on the lives of girls and women is one of the major issues in the Taliban's international relationships and that has cost them. Five years on, only one country, Russia, has formally recognised their rule.But when asked about this, Muttaqi points to the deepening diplomatic and economic ties with neighbours such as China and India, as well as Central Asian states. As for Kabul's relative isolation from western nations, he asks, "those who didn't have relationships with us over the past five years, what have they achieved?"He answers his own question: "Nothing."We heard that word - "nothing" - from every family we met at Zero Point, but in a much different sense. All were embarking on the hardest of homecomings, beginning all over again - with almost nothing.More on this story

articles.title: New storm names for 2026-2027 released by Met Office
articles.summary: Tuesday 1 September marks the start of the UK storm season and a new list of storm names have been released including Austen, Chloe and Evelyn.
articles.body: Storm names are selected jointly by the Met Office, Met Éireann and KNMI, with the final list aiming to reflect communities across the UK, Ireland and the Netherlands.In 2025 the three meteorology agencies invited nominations for names from the public.More than 40,000 were submitted  - we saw names such as Amy, Isla and Marty selected for the 2025/2026 storm season.This year's list continues to draw on those suggestions, reflecting not only popular choices, but also some of the personal stories behind them.For example Austen was suggested in honour of Austen Nagle, the first director of the Irish Meteorological Service.Chloe was selected by the Met Office after being nominated more than 130 times, including once by the mother of a five-year-old who is described by her  mum as "fascinated by the weather" but can also "create a storm by herself" when she is tired.And Ivy was nominated in honour of a nine-month-old Labrador puppy affectionately known as "the absolute destructor".Any remnant of a tropical storm or hurricane that crosses the Atlantic will keep its original name, for example ex-Hurricane Erin, which brought a large swell to South West England in August 2025 and was named 'Storm Erin'.To ensure consistency with the US National Hurricane Centre naming conventions, names that begin with the letters Q, U, X, Y and Z are not used.

articles.title: Magna increases bet on battery swapping in India with $35M for Yuma
articles.summary: Magna's investment in Yuma Energy has reached $87 million as the Canadian auto supplier increases its majority stake in the Indian battery-swapping firm.
articles.body:
While battery swapping has struggled to take off in much of the world, Canadian auto parts giant Magna International believes the model could work at scale in India, where millions of two- and three-wheelers and a fast-growing delivery economy create a different set of economics.
And it’s placing that bet on Yuma Energy, a Bengaluru-based firm that operates a battery-swapping network for electric two- and three-wheelers. Yuma, which spun out of Indian mobility startup Yulu in early 2023, has completed more than 60 million swaps to date and now has about 100,000 batteries deployed across its network.
Magna is now investing another $35 million in Yuma, increasing the auto supplier’s stake from the 51% it took when the joint venture was formed, Yuma managing director Muthu Subramanian said in an interview. As a result, Yulu’s 49% stake will be diluted. Subramanian declined to disclose the new ownership split.
Yulu and Yuma are Magna’s only startup investments in India, the company confirmed to TechCrunch. In 2022, Magna committed a combined $77 million to the two businesses, with $25 million going to Yulu and $52 million to the battery-swapping joint venture.
Betting on India’s gig economy
Magna’s latest investment hinges in large part on India’s growing gig economy.
Delivery riders can lose valuable time, and revenue, while charging their EVs. Subramanian estimates that only about 10% to 15% of vehicles used by gig workers in India are electric today, leaving considerable room for operators such as Yuma if more of those riders switch from gasoline-powered vehicles.
“With Indian gig workers’ high runtime on a daily basis, an EV makes absolute sense in terms of cost of ownership,” Subramanian told TechCrunch. “Uptime is important.”
Yuma is targeting those high-mileage riders, arguing that swapping is more practical than fast charging. A battery, Subramanian said, can be exchanged in under two minutes, while even a 20- or 30-minute fast charge takes a rider off the road and requires more space and power to serve multiple vehicles at once.
However, building that convenience is expensive, as Yuma has to keep its batteries and swapping infrastructure ready before enough riders arrive to fully utilize them. “It’s a capital-intensive business, and the unit economics will play out at scale,” Subramanian said.
Yuma is not profitable yet, though some of its older swapping stations are already EBITDA-positive, Subramanian said. The firm operates more than 400 stations with over 2,500 charging units and ended the financial year in March 2026 with about ₹1 billion (about $10.5 million) in revenue. It is targeting EBITDA break-even within the next two quarters, Subramanian told TechCrunch.
Getting there will still require Yuma to build ahead of demand. The firm plans to use the bulk of Magna’s investment to expand its swapping infrastructure and double its fleet of about 100,000 batteries over the next 12 to 18 months.
Yulu still accounts for the vast majority of Yuma’s 60 million lifetime swaps, though that dependence has started to ease as about 15% to 20% of swaps in the latest quarter came from customers other than Yulu, Subramanian said.
Beyond Yulu, Yuma now serves more than five fleets and has integrated its batteries with more than 10 vehicle platforms, including models from Kinetic Green, Motovolt, BGauss, and Quantum Energy. The firm expects non-Yulu customers to account for about 25% of its swaps within the next two years, Subramanian said.
Earlier this month, Yulu raised $93 million to grow its electric two-wheeler fleet. Yuma will therefore need to expand its network to keep pace with its largest customer and accommodate newer fleets using its batteries.
Yuma operates its battery-swapping network across 18 Indian cities, including Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Mumbai, and the Delhi region, as well as Jaipur, Lucknow, Indore, Coimbatore, Kochi, and Kolkata. With the fresh capital, the firm plans to expand into Chennai and Pune in the coming quarters while adding more stations in cities where it already operates.
India will remain Yuma’s focus for at least the next 12 to 18 months. However, Subramanian told TechCrunch that the firm plans to take the model overseas as part of its longer-term roadmap. Southeast Asian markets, including Vietnam and Thailand, as well as parts of Africa, could be attractive because of their large two-wheeler markets, he said, though Yuma has yet to begin discussions about entering them.
Unlike operators that simply run swapping networks, Yuma designs and manufactures its own battery packs and charging units. The firm makes battery packs at its facility in Chennai and charging units in Bengaluru, giving it control over both the hardware and the network that manages them.

articles.body: In our story contest, we ask people to imagine the future, evenly distributed.The AI revolution has only just begun to affect humanity, and billions of humans have yet to so much as talk to a frontier LLM like Fable or Sol. This is in large part because compute limitations make it impossible to serve the highest-quality AIs to more than a relative handful of users: humanity is GPU-poor. Only a few million GPUs capable of efficiently serving frontier models are manufactured annually.This will increase, however, as both hardware and software are scaled and optimized. Someday, such as in 2040, there may be available, for every human being, the performance equivalent of 'a B300 GPU for contemporary LLMs'.What would this world be like?What will our world be like when (not if) every human being has access to the equivalent of a Fable or Sol LLM 24/7/365? Will this lead to a panopticon of indefatigable AI surveillance? Will education be revolutionized by infinitely patient tutors? Will social media cease to exist as we know it? Will healthcare be revolutionized by world class AI doctors and personalized medicines? What will happen in the oft-ignored developing world?AI as we know it already holds the potential to be far more transformative than the smartphone or perhaps even the Internet itself.We invite you to imagine this 'mundane' future.PremiseImagine that AI frontier progress stops as of 1 September 2026: AI becomes faster and cheaper, but it never becomes superhuman or improves considerably across the board.So the Singularity never happens—but GPUs keep getting made. By 2040, there may be the equivalent of 8 billion GPUs globally and everyone has access to a frontier LLM.What happens in this 'business as usual' future?

articles.title: Burnham to face Parliament as prime minister for first time
articles.summary: This may well be the point when his honeymoon period as PM ends and the hard work begins, Damian Grammaticas writes.
articles.body: Andy Burnham is set to speak in the Commons later, addressing MPs on their first day back at work after the summer recess, in what will be a highly charged moment.Six weeks after he walked up Downing Street, and 16 years after he last appeared at the dispatch box as part of a Labour government, he will stand before MPs for the first time as prime minister.In the close confines of the chamber, with ranks of Labour members behind him, Burnham will finally come face to face with his political opponents.The pressure of the occasion, the scrutiny he will face, the deftness with which he handles questions, the attacks, the barbs, the asides, will all be key to how the public perceive him.Downing Street does not want to give too much away but we know he will meet his cabinet before delivering a statement "setting out the direction of his government" and facing questions from MPs.A Number 10 source said over the weekend that Burnham did not want his government to "stand by and watch on as every bill goes up and up".So he "will promise the country that wherever we can make life more affordable we will".Burnham has had a relatively easy summer. When he became prime minister, MPs were already on their break.So he has been free to travel the country unveiling policies designed to help with the cost of living: a £2 cap on bus fares; removing VAT from domestic energy bills; and cutting business rates for pubs, clubs and music venues by 20% next year.But now the challenges he will face having ousted Sir Keir Starmer begin. And there is an autumn packed with political tests coming.There will be his first session of Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, then the spotlight of the party conferences, his first Budget and, later in the year, a speech where he will lay out a 10-year plan for the country.It is thought this week he may say more about his plans to bring privatised services back under public control, arguing that doing so will help ease the pressure on family budgets.Number 10 says Burnham will tell MPs he will keep taking action on the cost of living.The Conservatives and Reform UK, however, are preparing to attack his policies, questioning how they will be funded and whether there will be new tax rises.Kemi Badenoch reshuffled her shadow cabinet team on Monday in preparation for this moment. To sharpen her party's attacks on Labour over its handling of tax and the economy she promoted Andrew Griffith to be her new shadow chancellor.The Conservatives are making much of his past jobs in business. Before entering politics he was chief financial officer and chief operating officer at Sky, and chair of Just Eat.He is promising a Conservative government that would deliver "lower, simpler taxes, get Britain drilling again to bring down energy costs, slash the red tape holding Britain back, and scrap the job-killing measures in Labour's (Un)Employment Rights Act".Labour and the Liberal Democrats have seized on the fact Griffith was a Treasury minister in Liz Truss's government and publicly defended her "mini-budget".Bridget Phillipson, the Labour Party chair, said the "Tories' top team is crammed full of the same vandals who hammered family finances and left our public services crumbling".Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said Griffith's appointment showed the Conservatives were "happy to forfeit any claim to economic credibility".Burnham will face criticism from the Greens too. Their leader, Zack Polanski, says that Burnham's ideas for greater public control over vital services is "just tinkering".Polanski says "if he really wants to bring back hope, he needs to tax the wealthy, take water and energy back under public ownership, bring in rent controls, and say no to new North Sea drilling".The Liberal Democrats are already attacking Burnham's plans to deal with the prisons crisis.Their justice spokesperson, Jess Brown-Fuller, said Labour's promise to build new cells was not backed by any new money and proved "just how unserious this Government remains about fixing our justice system".Other major challenges facing Burnham include defence. How will he fund the plans he has inherited from Sir Keir? And, beyond that, how fast will he increase spending to meet Nato commitments?There are imminent decisions to be made about whether to approve new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea. There are looming choices about whether to do more to help as energy bills rise this winter, whether to increase taxes at the Budget. And longer-term issues about reforms to welfare, social care and ties with the EU.All of which means that the moment when Burnham rises to address MPs on Tuesday may well be the point when his honeymoon period as prime minister ends and the hard work begins.

articles.title: RotaryCell: Making an unmodified rotary phone work over LTE with an ESP32-S3
articles.summary:
Article URL: https://github.com/fregacmols/RotaryCell
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49517297
Points: 127
# Comments: 34
articles.body:
RotaryCell converts a traditional rotary telephone into a self-contained, battery-powered, portable cellular telephone without modifying the original telephone.
The design continues to use the original handset, rotary dial, switch-hook, mechanical ringer, network block, and existing jacks. The added electronics mount reversibly inside the case; no original telephone parts need to be drilled, cut, or permanently altered.
The working prototype can be carried and operated away from a fixed telephone connection, making the original desk telephone usable at meetings, demonstrations, or anywhere compatible cellular service is available.
This is a working engineering archive rather than a finished construction release. The hand-wired prototype operates, while the first integrated PCBs are currently awaiting assembly and validation.
Reproduce the working prototype by hand
The complete point-to-point wiring and component reference is the primary starting point for recreating the proven hand-wired prototype:
Open or download the full-resolution printable PDF. It covers the LilyGO, protected 21700, passive audio components, AG1171, GPIO connections, and original Model 500 circuitry without using the new PCBs. A hand-wired installation fits inside the telephone, but arranging and insulating all of the loose components and wiring is challenging; expect repeated dry-fitting and careful routing.
This repository records the project as it stood on August 28, 2026:
Firmware v0.10.4 is the current prototype-tested software.
The Audio and Reset A4 PCB was ordered from JLCPCB on August 27, 2026.
The AG1171 Carrier Through-Hole PCB was ordered from JLCPCB on August 28, 2026.
Both ordered PCB packages are archived exactly as submitted and have not yet been validated as assembled boards.
See STATUS.md for the distinction between tested prototype behavior and hardware awaiting validation.
A LilyGO T-A7670G-S3 Standard board supplies the ESP32-S3 controller, A7670 cellular modem, battery charging, and cellular audio interface.
A Silvertel AG1171 subscriber-line interface operates the telephone line circuitry, senses the switch-hook, and drives the mechanical ringer.
The Audio and Reset A4 PCB provides adjustable transmit/receive audio conditioning and a hardware power-cycle circuit for recovery when software-only modem reset is insufficient.
A single protected 21700 cell connects to the LilyGO battery pads through a harness in place of the original 18650 holder and directly supplies the AG1171 carrier VPWR input.
The telephone's RJ11 line jack is used only to deliver regulated 5 V to the LilyGO charging input on the designated pins. It does not power the AG1171 directly and is not used as a telephone-line interface.
Current Arduino sketch and source files
Current application OTA binary and source ZIP
Exact Audio and Reset A4 source and manufacturing package
Exact through-hole carrier source and Gerber package
Material associated with the working hand-wired prototype
Unfinalized schematics, layouts, libraries, and alternatives
Older hardware documentation retained for reference
Architecture, bring-up, and historical documentation
Draft project-page copy for evilroot.net
For a hand-wired build, start with the complete prototype wiring reference. For the newer PCB implementation, continue with STATUS.md, current hardware wiring, the master BOM, the assembly guide, and BUILDING.md.
Rotary pulse dialing and switch-hook detection
Incoming and outgoing cellular calls
Physical bell ringing through the AG1171
North American dial, reorder, and receiver-off-hook warning tones
Bidirectional handset audio with adjustable levels
USB diagnostics and a temporary maintenance Wi-Fi dashboard
Browser/USB AT-command terminal and persistent event log
Cellular-network clock synchronization and application OTA updates
Dial service code 0000 starts maintenance Wi-Fi. Service code 9999 performs modem diagnostics and software recovery, but it did not recover the field-observed modem lockup described in STATUS.md.
Never connect prototype Tip/Ring wiring or the repurposed charging jack to the public telephone network or energized premises telephone wiring.
Clearly label the charging jack and verify its regulated voltage, polarity, pin assignment, and protection before use.
Lithium-ion cells require suitable protection, charging, fusing, insulation, and mechanical restraint.
The maintenance access point uses the development password rotarycell. Change WIFI_AP_PASSWORD in Config.h before use around untrusted people.
The August 2026 PCB files are as ordered, not yet production-tested. Create a new revision rather than silently replacing an as-ordered package.
This is a public engineering and development archive. It is intended to preserve a durable, reproducible baseline, make the working hand-wired prototype available to other builders, and document progress toward a more integrated implementation.
The repository should not be mistaken for a finished construction kit or production release. Files under hardware/audio-reset-a4 and hardware/ag1171-carrier-through-hole record the exact board candidates ordered in August 2026; their assembled operation has not yet been validated. Tested behavior, known failures, and remaining documentation gaps are tracked in STATUS.md.
